transcript:
Nurse -> Northstar Home Health, this is Priscilla.
Caller -> Hi. This is Terrence Obuya. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi, Terrence. Your date of birth?
Caller -> June eighth, nineteen sixty nine.
Nurse -> And I have five one two, five five five, zero one six seven.
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> What's going on?
Caller -> My incision is itchy. On my knee, the right one. It's been two days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there any redness, or any drainage?
Caller -> No. It looks good. No redness, no drainage.
Nurse -> Any fever?
Caller -> No. I took it this morning. Ninety eight point four.
Nurse -> That's reassuring. Itching around a healing incision is really common. It usually means the skin is healing.
Caller -> Oh good. I was worried.
Nurse -> Try not to scratch it. If it bothers you, tap it or press lightly. Keep the area clean and dry, and wear loose clothes over it.
Caller -> Okay. Tap, not scratch. Got it.
Nurse -> Your nurse is scheduled to see you Monday morning. She'll look at it then.
Caller -> Monday. Okay.
Nurse -> If you see redness, swelling, or warmth, or any drainage, or you get a fever of one hundred point four or higher, call us.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> How's the knee feeling otherwise? Are you doing your exercises?
Caller -> Yes. Twice a day. It's stiff in the morning but it loosens up. I can bend it almost to ninety degrees now.
Nurse -> That's great progress for two weeks. Keep it up, and keep the ice on afterwards.
Caller -> I will. My wife helps me with the ice packs.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Ana.
Caller -> Hi, Ana. It's Paolo. I'm calling about my son, Nico. N I C O. Marchetti.
Nurse -> Hi, Paolo. Nico's date of birth?
Caller -> April third, twenty nineteen.
Nurse -> And I have three four seven, five five five, zero one eight five for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on?
Caller -> It's his trach. He has a lot more secretions. For the last two days.
Caller -> I'm suctioning him about every two hours now. Before, it was every four.
Nurse -> Okay. What color are the secretions?
Caller -> Clear. Thin and clear. Not yellow, not green.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. I took it a few minutes ago. Ninety eight point six.
Nurse -> Okay, good. And how's his breathing? Is he working hard to breathe?
Caller -> No, no. His breathing is easy. His color is good. He's playing with his trains right now. He's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he coughing?
Caller -> A little. A mild cough. Just when the secretions build up.
Nurse -> Okay. That all sounds reassuring. Clear secretions, no fever, and breathing easily. Sometimes the secretions go up when the air is dry, or when he's coming down with a cold.
Caller -> He did have the sniffles on Sunday. Maybe that's it.
Nurse -> It could be. Is his humidifier working?
Caller -> I think so. The heated one, the one that attaches to the trach. Let me look. Yes. It's on. The water is low, though. I'll refill it.
Nurse -> Good idea. Keep it filled. And give him extra fluids, as much as he'll take.
Caller -> He loves juice. I'll give him some.
Nurse -> Perfect. Suction him as needed, whenever he sounds wet or coughs. And write down the color and amount, so we can see if it changes.
Caller -> I'll keep notes. Okay.
Nurse -> I'd like our respiratory therapist to see him tomorrow, just to check everything. Humidification, the trach tube, and his secretions.
Caller -> That would be great. What time?
Nurse -> Tomorrow afternoon. She'll call you before she comes.
Caller -> Okay. Tomorrow afternoon. I'm home all day.
Nurse -> Now, you mentioned you're running low on something?
Caller -> Oh, yes. Suction catheters. I have about six left. At this rate, that's just a couple of days.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me order those now. What size does he use?
Caller -> Ten French. Same as always.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll put in an order for ten French catheters. They should come tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, use a fresh catheter each time, as usual. If you run short before they come, call me and I'll see about getting a few from the on-call stock.
Caller -> I will. That's good to know.
Nurse -> If his secretions turn yellow or green, or have blood, or he gets a fever, or he's working harder to breathe, call us. And if he turns blue, or the tube is blocked and you can't clear it, call nine one one.
Caller -> Yellow, green, blood, fever, harder breathing. And nine one one if blue or blocked. I know the drill.
Nurse -> You do. You're a pro.
Caller -> It's been four years. I guess I'd better be.
Nurse -> And how are the nights? Is the pulse oximeter on while he sleeps?
Caller -> Yes. Every night. It reads ninety seven, ninety eight. No alarms in the last few days, thankfully.
Nurse -> That's great. Keep it on. And who's covering overnight?
Caller -> My wife and I take turns. We alternate nights. It's tiring, but we manage.
Nurse -> You're both amazing. Tell your wife I said so.
Caller -> I will. She'll appreciate that. She always says you're her favorite.
Nurse -> Ha. Mutual. How's Nico doing at school? Is he going in person?
Caller -> He's going three days a week. His teacher is amazing. She learned to suction him, and she has a nurse in the classroom too.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Is he enjoying it?
Caller -> He loves it. He has a best friend, Marcus. They sit together and build things. The two of them are always making trains out of blocks.
Nurse -> Ha. That's so sweet. Does he have a favorite?
Caller -> The big blue one, Thomas. He sleeps with him at night. Thomas goes everywhere.
Nurse -> Perfect. Well, tell him I said hello.
Caller -> I will. He'll want to say hi himself, he always asks for you.
Nurse -> Ha. Put him on.
Caller -> Hang on. Nico, say hi to Ana. He's shaking his head. He's shy today.
Nurse -> That's okay. Hello, Nico. I'll see you soon.
Caller -> He waved. Okay. Thank you, Ana.
Caller -> Oh, before I go. His sister has a recital Saturday and he wants to go. Is that okay with the secretions?
Nurse -> It should be fine if he's well and you bring the suction machine and supplies. Sit near the back so you can step out.
Caller -> That's the plan. We'll bring the whole kit.
Nurse -> Perfect. Take care, Paolo.

Caller -> Hi, this is Kyle from the call center. I have a daughter on the line for a patient. The patient is Lorena Quintero. Q U I N T E R O.
Nurse -> Okay, Kyle. Go ahead and transfer.
Caller -> Okay. Here she comes.
Caller -> Hello? Hi. This is Camila. I'm her daughter.
Nurse -> Hi, Camila. What's your mother's date of birth?
Caller -> September thirtieth, nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> And your number, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> Seven eight six, five five five, zero one six eight.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on?
Caller -> So my mom is up two pounds. Since yesterday. She weighs herself every morning, like the nurse told her.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she short of breath?
Caller -> No. No, she's breathing fine. She's sitting up in her chair, eating a banana.
Nurse -> Okay. Any swelling?
Caller -> A little in her ankles. A little more than usual.
Nurse -> Okay. What did she eat yesterday?
Caller -> We had a family dinner. She had soup, and ham. The ham was salty. I told her.
Nurse -> That might be part of it. Okay. For today, low salt meals. No canned soup or deli meat. And she can have her fluids as her doctor allows.
Caller -> Okay. No soup, no ham. I'll make her oatmeal and an egg.
Nurse -> And keep weighing every morning, after she uses the bathroom and before she eats. Write it down.
Caller -> She does that already. I'll check the paper.
Nurse -> If she gains three pounds in a day, or five in a week, or the swelling gets worse, or she's short of breath, call us. And if she can't catch her breath, nine one one.
Caller -> Three in a day, five in a week. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call tomorrow morning to see her weight.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you, Beth.

transcript:
Nurse -> Juniper Ridge Hospice, this is Lena.
Caller -> Hi, Lena. This is Helen Ostrowski. I'm calling about my husband, Walter.
Nurse -> Hi, Helen. Walter's date of birth?
Caller -> June fifteenth, nineteen forty.
Nurse -> And I have five one three, five five five, zero one nine oh for you.
Caller -> Yes, that's the house phone. Everybody uses it.
Nurse -> How is Walter doing?
Caller -> He's sleeping a lot. A whole lot. About twenty hours a day, I'd say, now. For about five days.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he wake up at all?
Caller -> A little. For a few minutes. He'll open his eyes, say a word or two. Mostly he sleeps.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he eating or drinking?
Caller -> Hardly anything. A few sips of water. And two spoonfuls of ice cream today. That's all.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he in pain?
Caller -> I don't think so. He's not grimacing, he's not moaning. He looks peaceful.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good.
Caller -> Oh, hold on. Danny! Danny, can you take the kids outside? Grandpa is sleeping. Thank you, honey. Sorry, Lena. That's my grandson. They're all here.
Nurse -> Oh, that's lovely. How many are there?
Caller -> Our three children, and five grandchildren, and a couple of spouses. It's a full house. I've been cooking for an army.
Nurse -> Ha. It sounds wonderful. And exhausting.
Caller -> Both. Yes. I'm tired, I'll admit it. But it means so much that they're here.
Nurse -> Helen, has there been any change in his breathing? Long pauses, or noisy breathing?
Caller -> Sometimes there are pauses. He'll stop for a few seconds, and then take a big breath. It scares the kids.
Nurse -> That's called Cheyne Stokes breathing. It's a common pattern near the end of life. It usually isn't uncomfortable for him, though it can be hard for the family to watch.
Caller -> That's what the other nurse said. It still scares me every time.
Nurse -> Of course it does. If it helps, you can tell the kids it's his body's way of settling down.
Caller -> I'll tell them. My youngest, Katie, is only seven. She keeps asking if Grandpa is cold.
Nurse -> A soft blanket is fine, if his hands feel cool. Hands and feet often feel cool near the end. It's circulation, not discomfort.
Caller -> I'll get the quilt his mother made. The blue one. He's had it since he was a boy.
Nurse -> That sounds perfect.
Nurse -> Is he passing urine?
Caller -> Less. The brief is only wet once or twice a day now. It's dark yellow.
Nurse -> That's expected, since he's drinking so little.
Caller -> Okay. I wondered about that.
Nurse -> Who is staying near him at night?
Caller -> Our oldest, Mark, sleeps on the couch next to the bed. And I check on him every hour or so.
Nurse -> Make sure you rest too. Let Mark and the others take turns.
Caller -> I'll try. It's hard to leave his side.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. This is Tamika, I'm a nurse at Cedar Crest Care Center. I'm calling about one of your residents. Lucille Armitage.
Nurse -> Hi, Tamika. Lucille's date of birth?
Caller -> December eighth, nineteen thirty three.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> The nurses' station. Seven oh four, five five five, zero one eight six.
Nurse -> Got it. What's going on with Lucille?
Caller -> I just took over from the day shift, and the report I got is confusing. I wanted to check with you. Her pain seems worse, and she's not eating well.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you know.
Caller -> So the day nurse said her pain was a three. A three out of ten. In her left hip. But when I went in to see her just now, she was grimacing, and she told me it's a six.
Nurse -> Okay. So three earlier, and six now.
Caller -> Right. Or I think the three was this morning, and the six was this evening. I'm not sure. The day nurse is gone, I can't ask her.
Nurse -> Okay. So the pain may have gone up during the day.
Caller -> Maybe. Or maybe she just reported it differently. I really don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. What about her eating?
Caller -> The aide said she ate about a quarter of her lunch. But the dietary sheet says she ate half. So I don't know which is right.
Nurse -> Okay. So between a quarter and half.
Caller -> Yes. I'm sorry that I can't be more precise.
Nurse -> No, that's fine, you're doing your best with what you have. Let me ask a few other things. Does she have a fever?
Caller -> No. I checked. Ninety eight point two.
Nurse -> Any falls?
Caller -> No falls.
Nurse -> Okay. What does she have for pain?
Caller -> She has oxycodone, five milligrams, every four hours as needed. The day nurse wrote that she gave one at two this afternoon.
Nurse -> Okay. So the last dose was at two. It's after eight now, so it's been more than four hours.
Caller -> Right. So she could have another.
Nurse -> Yes. Since she's grimacing, and the pain is at least moderate, I'd give the oxycodone now. As long as the pain is above a four, and it's been at least four hours, she can have it.
Caller -> Okay. It's above a four, for sure. I'll give it.
Nurse -> Good. And please start recording a pain score every four hours, along with her expression. Also, write down a percentage after each meal. That will help us see what's really going on.
Caller -> I can do that. I'll put a note on the chart, for all the shifts.
Nurse -> Perfect. Reposition her every two hours, with a pillow between the knees. And offer her favorite foods.
Caller -> She likes the pudding. And ice cream. I'll bring some.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll send a nurse to see her tomorrow morning, to look at both the pain and the intake.
Caller -> Oh good. That would help.
Nurse -> And I'll call you after the visit, to go over what she found.
Caller -> Okay. Tomorrow. I'm on again at seven.
Nurse -> Great. Then I'll call you around nine.
Caller -> Perfect.
Nurse -> If her pain goes over a seven, or she gets very sleepy, or runs a fever, or falls, call us right away.
Caller -> Okay. Over seven, sleepy, fever, fall. Got it.
Nurse -> Tamika, is she awake and alert, apart from the pain? Does she know who you are?
Caller -> She's alert. She knows me. She called me by name when I came in. She's a little tired, but she's oriented.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. And her bowels? When was the last movement?
Caller -> Yesterday, I think. I'd have to check the flow sheet. I can look when we hang up.
Nurse -> Please do, and let me know if it's more than three days.
Caller -> I will. We're short staffed tonight, so I'm covering two halls. I'm sorry if I sound rushed.
Nurse -> You sound great. We appreciate your calling when something seems off.
Caller -> Thank you. That means a lot, after a long shift.
Nurse -> Is she comfortable now?
Caller -> She's resting. She seems okay. I'll give the medicine and sit with her a minute.
Nurse -> That's nice of you. Does she have family who visit?
Caller -> Her granddaughter comes on Sundays. She brings her little dog. Lucille lights up when she sees that dog.
Nurse -> Aw. That sounds like good medicine too.
Caller -> It is. The whole floor loves when the dog comes.
Nurse -> Ha. Is it okay for the dog to visit, with the other residents?
Caller -> Oh yes. The facility has a pet policy. Therapy dogs and family pets are welcome.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Okay, Tamika. Thank you for calling, and for taking good care of her.
Caller -> Thank you, Tom. I'll write everything down. Goodnight.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Hi, Rhonda. This is Monica. I'm calling about my dad. Stefan Kowalski.
Nurse -> Hi, Monica. Stefan Kowalsky. And his date of birth?
Caller -> October twelfth, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your phone number?
Caller -> Two four eight, five five five, zero one eight seven.
Nurse -> Okay, got it. And what's going on with your father, Mr. Kovalski?
Caller -> He hasn't had a bowel movement in three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he having any pain in his belly?
Caller -> Some bloating. His belly feels full, and it's a little puffy. But not terrible pain.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he throwing up?
Caller -> No. No vomiting.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look at his orders. Okay. He recently had the hip repair, right?
Caller -> Yes. Two weeks ago. He's been on the pain pills, and he's not moving much. I think that's why.
Nurse -> That's very likely. Pain medicine and less movement both slow the bowels. I see MiraLAX on his list as needed. Do you have it?
Caller -> We do. At home. I haven't used it. I wasn't sure if I should.
Nurse -> What is he taking for pain right now?
Caller -> The oxycodone. Five milligrams, twice a day. He says it helps.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he using it every day?
Caller -> Every day, morning and night. He hates to miss it.
Nurse -> That may be contributing to the constipation.
Caller -> I figured. Should he stop it?
Nurse -> No, not on your own. Keep giving it as prescribed, and let's treat the constipation. The surgeon can adjust the pain plan if needed.
Caller -> Okay. I won't stop it.
Nurse -> And how's his appetite?
Caller -> He's eating less, because he feels full. A few bites at a time.
Nurse -> Okay. That fits with the constipation too. I'd go ahead and give him one capful of the MiraLAX today, in eight ounces of water or juice.
Caller -> One capful. Okay. In juice is fine?
Nurse -> Juice is fine.
Nurse -> It's the bottle on the bathroom shelf, I think.
Caller -> Okay. The bathroom shelf. I'll find it. Thank you.
Nurse -> And a lot of fluids, like water, and prune juice, and fiber, like fruit and oatmeal. And short walks with the walker, every couple of hours.
Caller -> He walks to the kitchen and back. I'll get him to do more.
Nurse -> That's great. I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow, to check on his bowels, and look at how he's doing.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll send a message to his surgeon about the constipation, since it's after surgery.
Caller -> Okay. I would appreciate that.
Nurse -> If he starts throwing up, or his belly gets hard and swollen, or he has severe pain, or he hasn't gone within twenty four hours after the MiraLAX, call us right away.
Caller -> Okay. Vomiting, hard belly, severe pain, or twenty four hours. Got it.
Nurse -> How is he doing otherwise? Is he eating?
Caller -> He's eating less, because he feels full. But he's drinking. He's a little grumpy, to be honest. He hates being stuck at home.
Nurse -> That's understandable. Is he doing his physical therapy?
Caller -> The therapist comes twice a week. He likes her. He calls her the drill sergeant.
Nurse -> Ha. Those are the best ones.
Caller -> He says she's the only person who makes him move. I told him that's her job.
Nurse -> Ha. And a good one. How are you holding up, Monica? You sound like you're doing a lot.
Caller -> I'm okay. I live forty minutes away, so I come three or four times a week. My brother lives closer. He does the weekends.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good plan. Is your father alone during the week?
Caller -> Mostly. He has a neighbor, Mr. Okafor, who checks on him. And a medical alert button he wears around his neck.
Nurse -> That's good. Does he wear it all the time?
Caller -> I make him. He complains that it's itchy. I bought him a softer cord, and that helped.
Nurse -> Perfect. Safety first. Is there a rug or anything he could trip on?
Caller -> I took the rugs out. And my brother put in a grab bar in the bathroom last weekend.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. You've thought of everything.
Caller -> I'm trying. It's a lot, but we manage. He's a stubborn man, but he's a good man. He was a machinist for forty years.
Nurse -> A machinist! So he's used to precision and doing things right.
Caller -> Ha. That's why he's so particular about his recovery. He tracks his own steps on a little notepad.
Nurse -> I love that. Tell him the nurse will want to see the notepad tomorrow.
Caller -> He'll be thrilled. He'll probably give a presentation.

turns.speaker: Caller

Caller -> Tonight? Oh, thank you. Thank God.

Caller -> Okay. Thank you. That would be so good.

Nurse -> That's fine. The nurse will check that when she comes. Is her mouth dry?
Caller -> A little. We've been using the swabs. And I put some of that lip balm on her.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly right.
Caller -> My mom is the one who knows everything. I'm just helping. She does the nights, usually, but she's been up for two days straight, so I told her to rest.

Caller -> That's what I'm hoping. Okay.

Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay.

Caller -> She loves gospel. I have it on my phone. I'll play it softly.
Nurse -> Perfect. And don't argue with her about what she sees. If she wants to talk to Joseph, let her. Just stay calm.
Caller -> I won't argue. I just say, he's here, Grandma. I sit with her.
Nurse -> That's exactly right. Keep the bed low, and stay close.
Caller -> I'm right next to her.
Nurse -> And if she becomes combative, or hard to wake up, or has trouble breathing, call me right away.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> How are you holding up, Tamar? It's late.
Caller -> I'm okay. I work from home, so it's easier for me to stay. I'm a graphic designer. I've been designing a logo for a bakery. At least when I'm sitting here I can sketch.
Nurse -> That sounds like a nice way to pass the hours.

Nurse -> Ha. What a tribute.
Caller -> I know. She'd love that. She's the one who taught me to draw, actually. She used to sketch flowers in the margins of her church bulletin.
Nurse -> That's such a lovely thing. Maybe you can show her the logo.
Caller -> I will. I'll show her tomorrow. Maybe she'll be more awake.
Nurse -> I hope so.
Caller -> Hang on, someone's at the door. It's my aunt. Oh, she heard the phone. Hi, Auntie. Yes, it's the nurse. They're sending someone. Okay. She's going to sit with Grandma while I finish the call.
Nurse -> That's good. Is your mother up now?
Caller -> Yes. She woke up when Auntie came in. She's checking on Grandma. She says thank you.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Tell her I'll call in thirty minutes.
Caller -> I will. Thank you again, Tom.

Nurse -> It's up to you and your mother. If you feel the family would want to be here, it's a good time to let them know, so they can decide. I'm not saying it's tonight, but she is declining.
Caller -> I understand. I'll talk to my mom when she wakes up. I think she'll want to call them tomorrow.
Nurse -> That sounds right. And the nurse who comes tonight can talk with her about what to expect, too.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. Thank you for being honest.

Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you so much.

Nurse -> Juniper Ridge Hospice, this is Lena.
Caller -> Hi, Lena. This is Calvin Faircloth. I'm calling about my mother, Winona.
Nurse -> Hi, Calvin. Winona's date of birth?
Caller -> January ninth, nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And your number is six oh one, five five five, zero one nine two?
Caller -> That's me.
Nurse -> What can I do for you?
Caller -> So the comfort kit came this afternoon. The delivery guy dropped off a box. And I want to make sure I understand it before I need it. I don't want to mess up.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Let's go through it together. How is your mother doing right now?
Caller -> She's sleeping. Comfortably. She's not in pain, and she's breathing fine. She sleeps most of the day now, this whole week.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. So this is preparation. Do you have the kit in front of you?
Caller -> Yes. I have it open on the kitchen table. There are four bottles, and a few syringes, and a sheet of instructions.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's take them one at a time. Pick up the first bottle, and read me the label.
Caller -> Okay. The first one says morphine sulfate. Oral solution. Twenty milligrams per milliliter.
Nurse -> Good. And below that, do you see the directions?
Caller -> It says, point two five milliliters under the tongue every two hours as needed for pain or shortness of breath.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's the morphine. You'll use it if your mother seems to be in pain, like grimacing or moaning, or if her breathing looks hard. A quarter of a milliliter, which is a very small amount, and it goes between her cheek and her gum, or under her tongue.
Caller -> A quarter of a mil. That's tiny.
Nurse -> It is. It's a concentrated medicine. Use the syringe that came with it, not a kitchen spoon.
Caller -> Okay. The syringe with the little markings.
Nurse -> Right. And always write down the time of every dose.
Caller -> I have a notebook on the table. I'll start tonight.
Nurse -> Perfect. Next bottle.
Caller -> The second one says lorazepam. Point five milligram. Tablets. Under the tongue, every four hours as needed for anxiety or restlessness.
Nurse -> Right. That's the lorazepam. If she seems anxious, restless, or can't settle, that's what you'd use. It dissolves under the tongue.
Caller -> What's the difference between that and the morphine? How do I know which one?
Nurse -> Good question. Morphine is for pain and for the feeling of breathlessness. The lorazepam is for anxiety and restlessness. If she seems to be hurting, morphine. If she seems unsettled or worried, lorazepam. Sometimes you can use both.
Caller -> Okay. Pain, breathing, morphine. Restless, anxious, lorazepam.
Nurse -> Exactly right.
Caller -> What if I can't tell?
Nurse -> Then call us. That's what we're here for. We'll help you decide.
Caller -> Okay. That makes me feel better.
Nurse -> Next bottle.
Caller -> Third one. Haloperidol. Point five milligram. Every six hours as needed for agitation, nausea, or confusion.
Nurse -> Right. The haloperidol. That's for agitation or confusion, when she's restless in a way that's different from anxiety, like picking at the sheets, or seeing things that aren't there. It's also used for nausea.
Caller -> Okay. So that's the one if she gets confused.
Nurse -> Yes. Or if she's nauseous.
Caller -> Got it.
Nurse -> Last bottle.
Caller -> It's a little dropper bottle. Atropine. One percent. Two drops under the tongue, every four hours as needed for secretions.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the atropine. Near the end of life, sometimes a person gets noisy, gurgling breathing, because they can't clear their saliva. This dries the secretions. It's for the family's comfort as much as hers.
Caller -> Gurgling. Oh. Okay. I've heard that. Is it painful for her?
Nurse -> Usually it's not painful for the patient. It sounds worse than it feels. But the drops can help.
Caller -> Two drops, under the tongue. Okay.
Nurse -> Right. Calvin, you're doing great.
Caller -> I'm trying. Honestly, I'm afraid of giving the wrong one, or too much.
Nurse -> I understand. That's very common. That's why I'd like our nurse to come tomorrow, and show you in person how to give each one.
Caller -> That would be great. What time?
Nurse -> Tomorrow at eleven. She'll bring a practice syringe, and you can try it with water.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll be here. My sister is coming too, she wants to learn.
Nurse -> Wonderful. The more family members who know, the better. And keep the kit in one place, away from children and pets. Put our phone number on top of the box.
Caller -> I'll write it on a piece of tape. Right on the lid.
Nurse -> Perfect. And remember, you can call us any time, day or night, before you give anything, if you're not sure.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Caller -> Can I ask a couple more questions? What if she can't swallow anything at all?
Nurse -> Good question. These are all made to absorb in the mouth, between the cheek and gum or under the tongue, so she doesn't need to swallow. That's why we use them at this stage.
Caller -> Oh, that's reassuring. I was worried about that.
Caller -> And what if I give one and it doesn't seem to work?
Nurse -> Give it time. Most of them take fifteen to thirty minutes to work. If she's still uncomfortable after thirty minutes, call us, and we'll tell you what to do next.
Caller -> Fifteen to thirty minutes. Okay. I'll watch the clock.
Caller -> And what do I do with them when we're done? After.
Nurse -> The nurse will help you with that. We'll take care of the disposal. You don't need to worry about it now.
Caller -> Okay. I'm just trying to think of everything.
Nurse -> You're doing great. This is a lot to take in.
Nurse -> Any other questions about the kit?
Caller -> Just one. How do I know if she's comfortable? She can't tell me.
Nurse -> Good question. Look for a relaxed face, relaxed hands, and slow, easy breathing. If you see frowning, groaning, or restlessness, those are signs she may need something.
Caller -> Okay. A relaxed face is good. Frowning is not.
Nurse -> Right.
Caller -> My sister says our mother used to hum when she was content. Like, in the kitchen. We haven't heard it in a while.
Nurse -> That's a lovely sign to listen for. Maybe you'll hear it again.
Caller -> I hope so. She hummed hymns. Old ones. Her favorite was Amazing Grace.
Nurse -> It's a beautiful one. Maybe play it softly for her.
Caller -> I will. I'll put it on tonight.
Nurse -> And Calvin, how are you doing? This is a lot.
Caller -> It is. I took leave from work, and I'm staying here. I'm tired, but I'm okay. I'm glad I can be here.
Nurse -> That's a gift, for her and for you.
Caller -> Thank you. I needed to hear that. Alright. I'll let you go.
Nurse -> One more thing. Does anyone else live in the home, or visit? Any children, any pets?
Caller -> My sister is here. Her kids visit on weekends. They're six and nine. And my mother has a cat, Pepper. She sleeps on the bed with her.
Nurse -> Then please keep the box up high, on a shelf or in a cabinet, away from the kids and Pepper.
Caller -> I'll put it on top of the refrigerator. They can't reach that.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Take care, Calvin. See you tomorrow, well, the nurse will.
Caller -> Ha. Thanks, Lena. One more silly thing, can I tell my mom that you said hello? She won't hear, but I'd like to.
Nurse -> Please do. Tell her Lena says hello, and that we're thinking of her.
Caller -> I will. I'll tell her tonight when I put the hymn on.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely. Good night, Calvin.
Caller -> Good night.

Nurse -> Northstar Home Health, this is Priscilla.
Caller -> Hi, Priscilla. This is Josephine Arbuckle. I'm a patient. I'm sorry it's so late.
Nurse -> Hi, Josephine. Don't apologize. We're here all night. Can I get your date of birth?
Caller -> November second, nineteen eighty.
Nurse -> And a number for you? I have four oh four, five five five, zero one nine four.
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> What's going on tonight?
Caller -> I can't sleep. I haven't been able to sleep for weeks. I lie there, and my mind just races.
Nurse -> How much are you sleeping, would you say?
Caller -> Maybe three hours. If I'm lucky.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds exhausting.
Caller -> It is. And I'm just, I'm so tired of everything. The treatments, the appointments. The fear.
Nurse -> Of course you are. You've been through so much. How long since the diagnosis?
Caller -> Four months. It feels like four years.
Nurse -> Okay. How have you been feeling emotionally?
Caller -> Honestly? Not good. I don't enjoy anything anymore. Not my garden, not my books. I used to love my garden. Now I just look out the window and feel nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That's an important thing to say out loud.
Caller -> I haven't told anyone. Not even my husband.
Nurse -> I'm glad you told me. Josephine, I'd like to ask you something. Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or of not wanting to be here?
Caller -> Sometimes I wish I wouldn't wake up. In the morning.
Caller -> I'm not saying I'd do anything. It's not like that. I just, some nights I think, it would be easier if I didn't wake up.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for being so honest. That took courage. I'm really glad you called.
Caller -> I didn't plan to say that. It just came out.
Nurse -> I'm glad it did. I want to ask a few more questions, so I can understand and help. Is that okay?
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Do you have a plan? Have you thought about how you might do it?
Caller -> No. No plan. I haven't thought about that. I wouldn't know how.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have any guns in the house?
Caller -> No. We don't have any guns. My husband hates them.
Nurse -> Okay. And are you thinking of doing anything tonight?
Caller -> No. No, I'm not going to do anything. I just needed to talk. I couldn't talk to Dennis because he's at work.
Nurse -> Okay. Dennis is your husband?
Caller -> Yes. He works nights at the hospital. He's a respiratory therapist. He gets home around seven in the morning.
Nurse -> Okay. So you're alone right now.
Caller -> Yes. The house is so quiet at night.
Nurse -> Is there anyone else who could come and be with you? A friend, or family?
Caller -> My sister, Hannah. She lives about thirty minutes away.
Nurse -> Would you be okay if I called Hannah, with your permission?
Caller -> I don't want to wake her. She has two little kids.
Nurse -> I understand. But I think it would help to have someone with you tonight. And she'd want to know. Would you let me call her?
Caller -> I guess so. Okay. But can you call Dennis instead? He's at work, but he'd want to know. I'd feel better if he knew.
Nurse -> Of course. I can call Dennis. Is it okay if I tell him what you told me tonight?
Caller -> Yes. I want him to know. I just couldn't say it myself.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll call him as soon as we finish. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes. Thank you.
Nurse -> Josephine, what are you taking right now? Any medicines for mood?
Caller -> The sertraline. Fifty milligrams, once a day. They started it three weeks ago.
Nurse -> Okay. Has it helped?
Caller -> I don't notice a difference yet. Maybe I'm not giving it enough time.
Nurse -> It can take a few weeks. But I want your provider to know how you're doing, so they can adjust things if needed. I'm going to let them know tonight.
Caller -> I'd like that. I really would.
Nurse -> And I'm going to have our counselor call you today. She'll call within two hours. She's wonderful, she works with people going through cancer treatment, and she knows how heavy it can be.
Caller -> Okay. That sounds good. I'd like to talk to someone.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in thirty minutes, to check on you.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I want to give you a number, Josephine. Nine eight eight. It's a crisis line. You can call or text it any time, day or night. And if you ever form a plan, or you feel like you might act on the thoughts, call nine one one.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. Okay. I know that one. I never thought I'd need it.
Nurse -> You don't have to be in an emergency to call. Even if you're not sure.
Caller -> Okay. I understand.
Nurse -> And for tonight, please keep your medicines to just the daily amount, nothing extra. And if Dennis or Hannah can stay with you, that would be best.
Caller -> I only have what I take. I'll make sure it stays that way.
Nurse -> And if the thoughts get stronger tonight, you call us right away. Any time.
Caller -> Okay. I will.

Caller -> No. I don't want to make him feel worse. He's trying so hard.
Nurse -> Sometimes the person who loves us most wants to know exactly what we're feeling, even the hard parts. And I think he'd tell you that you are not a burden.
Caller -> He would. He says it all the time. But I don't believe him.
Nurse -> That makes sense when you're this tired. Depression and exhaustion tell us things that aren't true.

turns.text: No need to be sorry. Talk soon.

Nurse -> Cobalt Bay Home Health, this is Teodoro.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Teodoro. It's Philippa Okonkwo. I'm calling about my brother, Cordell. Cordell Hathaway.
Nurse -> Hi, Philippa. Can you spell his last name for me?
Caller -> H A T H A W A Y. Hathaway. It always gets turned into Hathaway with an E. People just assume.
Nurse -> Ha. Happens to everyone.
Caller -> Cordell just laughs it off. He says it's a family tradition.
Nurse -> Got it. H A T H A W A Y. Cordell Hathaway. What's going on?
Caller -> It's his mask. The BiPAP mask. The cushion part, the part that sits on his face, it's cracked and it's leaking air all night. And I need a new one.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has it been cracking?
Caller -> A few days. It was a little crack. Now it's, you can see through it. Along the side, by the nose.
Nurse -> Does he have a spare?
Caller -> We have one. But it's the wrong size. It's a medium and he wears a small. I don't know why they sent us a medium. It's been in the drawer since the spring.
Nurse -> Okay. So one cracked small, and one spare medium.
Caller -> Yes. That's all we have.
Nurse -> What's his date of birth, Philippa?
Caller -> September fourth, nineteen seventy three. He's fifty two. He's too young for this.
Nurse -> I'm so sorry. How is he sleeping?
Caller -> Not great. The leak makes a whistling sound, and it blows air in his eyes, and he keeps waking up. He's tired in the day.
Nurse -> Is he able to breathe comfortably when he's awake, off the machine?
Caller -> Yes. He's fine awake. He's sitting up right now doing his crossword. He doesn't seem short of breath.
Nurse -> Good to hear.
Nurse -> And is he with you?
Caller -> I'm at his house. I come over in the morning, I do his meds and breakfast. His wife works nights, so I cover. She's a nurse, actually.
Nurse -> Oh, that's a hard schedule.
Caller -> It is. They manage. He doesn't like asking for help. So I just show up.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sister.
Caller -> I try. He says I hover.
Nurse -> What number can I reach you at?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, zero one four three.
Nurse -> Four one four, five five five, zero one four three. Got it. And what brand is the mask? Is there a name on the box?
Caller -> Let me go look. Hang on, I have the box in the closet.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. It's a, uh, nasal mask. It says size small on the little tag. The cushion has a number, I can read it.
Nurse -> I don't need the number. I'll get it from the chart. I'll order a small cushion.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. A small. Not a medium.
Nurse -> Right. I'll order the small cushion for him.
Caller -> Okay. Good. How long will it take? Because tonight he's going to need to sleep.
Nurse -> I can get it to you tomorrow afternoon.
Caller -> Tomorrow afternoon. So tonight we're stuck with the leaky one.
Nurse -> Yes. For tonight use the cracked one. Make sure the chin strap is snug, and keep the head of the bed raised so it seals better. Don't use the medium. A wrong size will leak even worse.
Caller -> Cracked one. Snug strap. Head up. Don't use the medium. Okay.
Nurse -> And if the air leaks into his eyes, you can put a little tape on the crack from the outside. Only if you have to. A small piece of medical tape.
Caller -> I have the paper tape. I'll try that.
Nurse -> Good. Philippa, I also want to go over when to call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. Go ahead.
Nurse -> If he cannot get air, if his lips or face turn blue, or if he's hard to wake up, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Can't get air. Blue. Hard to wake. Nine one one. Yes. His wife told me the same thing.
Nurse -> Good. She'd know.
Caller -> She knows all of it. She keeps a list on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there anything else you need? Tubing? Filters?
Caller -> I think the filters are okay. I changed one last week. Tubing's fine. It's just the cushion.
Nurse -> Alright. Do you want me to have the delivery person call before they come?
Caller -> Yes. Call my cell. I'll let them in. Cordell sleeps late.
Nurse -> I'll note that.
Caller -> Thank you. I really appreciate it.
Nurse -> Anytime. We'll get him a good seal.
Caller -> I hope so. He needs his sleep. They said at the clinic that sleep helps. For the, you know. For the muscles.
Nurse -> It does. Rest is important.
Caller -> Yeah. I just don't want him to give up on the mask.
Nurse -> He won't. A good fit makes all the difference.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell him it's coming.
Nurse -> Tell him I said hello.
Caller -> I will. He likes you guys. He says the nurse with the bow tie is his favorite.
Nurse -> Ha. That would be Rafael. I'll tell him.
Caller -> Okay. Bye now.
Nurse -> Bye, Philippa.

Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Ingrid.
Caller -> Hi, Ingrid. It's Linus Ballantyne. I'm calling about my mom, Eugenia Ballantyne. She's on your service.
Nurse -> Hi, Linus. How can I help?
Caller -> I have a pill question. About her leg pain meds. I think I'm confused about which is which.
Nurse -> Sure. Let's sort it out together.
Caller -> Thanks. I've been staring at these bottles for twenty minutes.
Nurse -> That's what I'm here for. Which medicines are you looking at?
Caller -> There's two. One is the gabapentin. And one is the oxycodone. I've got the bottles on the counter.
Nurse -> Okay. Read me the gabapentin label.
Caller -> Gabapentin. One hundred milligrams. Three times a day. No wait. Hang on. Let me look at it again. I'm reading the wrong line. It's three hundred milligrams. Three hundred. Three times a day.
Nurse -> Three hundred milligrams, three times a day. Okay. When was her last dose?
Caller -> At noon. I gave it with her lunch.
Nurse -> Good. And the oxycodone?
Caller -> Oxycodone, five milligrams. Every four hours as needed for pain. It says one tablet.
Nurse -> When did she last have it?
Caller -> Two o'clock. Right after her nap. She said her leg was killing her. So I gave her one.
Nurse -> Okay. Did it help?
Caller -> Yes, some. She said it went from a seven to a five. But it's still there. It's a dull, throbby ache in the calf.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she sleepy? More sleepy than usual?
Caller -> No. She's awake. She's watching her game shows. She's, you know, she's herself. She's yelling at the contestants.
Nurse -> Does she get the answers right?
Caller -> Mostly. She's insufferable about it.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign.
Caller -> Yeah. She's got opinions.
Nurse -> What's her date of birth, Linus?
Caller -> November thirtieth, nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And your number in case I need to call back?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one five eight.
Nurse -> Got it. So what's your question exactly?
Caller -> I don't know which one she's supposed to take when. Like, the gabapentin, is that for the pain? Or is that a different thing? And can I give the oxycodone right now, because she's hurting again? It's almost five.
Nurse -> Good question. They work differently. The gabapentin is for nerve pain. She takes it three times a day, every day, on a schedule, whether or not she's hurting. It builds up and works over time.
Caller -> Okay. So that's not a, an as needed one.
Nurse -> Right. It's scheduled. The oxycodone is the as-needed. You give it only when she has pain, and there has to be at least four hours between doses.
Caller -> Four hours. Two o'clock, so, six o'clock.
Nurse -> Correct. It's almost five now, so she'd have to wait until after six.
Caller -> Okay. But she's hurting now. What do I do for the next hour?
Nurse -> Try a warm compress on the calf, keep the leg propped up, and see if she'd like a distraction. Is her next gabapentin due at dinner?
Caller -> Yes. At dinner. Around six.
Nurse -> That's fine. Give the gabapentin at dinner. You can give the oxycodone at six too, if she still needs it. It's safe to give them close together as long as she isn't very sleepy.
Caller -> At six. Both. If she needs it. Okay. And if she's sleepy?
Nurse -> Then skip the oxycodone and call us. Some people get drowsy when both are in their system.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense. I'll watch her.
Nurse -> Did you give any other medicine for the leg? Tylenol? Ibuprofen?
Caller -> No. Just those two.
Nurse -> Good. Please don't add any other pain pills without asking us.
Caller -> Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> I'm going to call you tomorrow morning to see how she did overnight.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. That's great. What time?
Nurse -> Between nine and ten.
Caller -> I'll be here. I work from home.
Nurse -> That helps. Is she alone when you're on calls?
Caller -> No, I set up in the living room next to her. She talks through my meetings.
Nurse -> Perfect. And Linus, call us if she gets very sleepy, confused, or if the pain stays high even after the oxycodone.
Caller -> Sleepy. Confused. Pain doesn't budge. Okay.
Nurse -> Is the leg swollen or red or warm?
Caller -> No. It looks the same as last week. The nurse looked at it on Monday.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring.
Caller -> Do you want me to write down the times? Like a log?
Nurse -> Yes, that's a great idea. Write the drug, the dose, and the time every time you give it.
Caller -> I have a notepad on the fridge. I'll put it there.
Nurse -> Good. Also keep both bottles on a high shelf, away from the TV tray.
Caller -> They are. I put them in the cabinet after each dose.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I'm sorry I got the gabapentin mixed up. I'm still learning all this.
Nurse -> You caught it yourself, Linus. That's exactly what we want. Always read the label twice.
Caller -> Twice. I'll make it a rule.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Ingrid.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk tomorrow.
Caller -> Bye.

turns.text: Well, the paper from the hospital. The discharge paper. It says forty. Forty milligrams, once a day. And I said, Ludmila, which is it? And she said she thinks it's, oh, I don't know, she said the little white one. Both of them are white.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. That doesn't help us much.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. They're twins.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: So the bottle says twenty and the hospital paper says forty.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yes. That's the whole thing. I don't know which to follow.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. Did she take it today?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: This morning. One tablet. From the bottle. I watched her.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: One tablet of the twenty.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I think so. I think. It's the bottle in the kitchen. It says twenty. I haven't checked if there's another bottle somewhere.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is there a pillbox, or just the bottles?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Just the bottles. She doesn't like the weekly boxes.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. That's helpful. How are her ankles?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Puffy. Both of them. She's got those, what do you call, sock marks. The marks where the socks dig in. And her shoes don't fit.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is the swelling worse than it was at discharge?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I can't say. I wasn't here last week. But it's not going down, that I can tell. Not yet.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does she have any trouble breathing? Lying flat, or walking across the room?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. No, she's breathing fine. She walked to the kitchen and back. She was a little tired. But no huffing.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Any chest pain?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Dizzy or lightheaded when she stands?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A little at the church picnic, she said. Not today.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. I need her date of birth to find her in our system.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Oh, goodness. Let me think. Hang on. It's on the, here, I have the paper. August fourteenth, nineteen thirty six.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: August fourteenth, nineteen thirty six. Thank you. And your number?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Nine oh one, five five five, zero one five one.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is that a cell?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: My home line. I have an answering machine, so leave a message if I'm out.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Got it, Hester. So here's the situation. I can't tell you over the phone which dose is right. I don't want to guess. Sometimes the hospital changes a dose at discharge and the pharmacy is still using the old bottle. Sometimes the paper is wrong.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Oh. So it could be either one.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It could. I need to check the actual order with her doctor's office. I'll call the discharging physician's office today to find out.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Oh, thank goodness. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Until we know, please give only what's on the bottle label. That's the pharmacy's most recent fill. One tablet of the twenty in the morning. Don't double up, and don't skip it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Just the bottle. The twenty. Okay. And not the forty.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Right. And keep the bottle and the discharge paper together so the clinician can look at both.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll put them in a bag. A plastic bag. On the table.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. I'll call you back by the end of the day once I know.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: By the end of the day. Okay. What if I don't hear?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Then call us again. Ask for me, Bettina.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Bettina. Okay. I'm writing it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. And Hester, your name again for the chart?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Hester. H E S T E R. Quill.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Another thing. Does she weigh herself?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I don't think so. There's a scale in the bathroom. Under the sink. It's covered in dust.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Wipe it off first.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I will. I'll bring a rag.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Could you have her step on it tomorrow morning, after she uses the bathroom, and write it down? Same time every day.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I can do that. I'll come by at nine.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Great. Call us right away if she has trouble breathing, any chest pain, or she gains more than a couple of pounds overnight. If she can't breathe or has chest pain, call nine one one.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Breathing. Chest pain. Weight gain. Nine one one for the first two. Okay.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does she have family nearby?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A niece in Ohio. She calls on Sundays. Mostly it's the church ladies. We take turns. I have Tuesday and Thursday.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's a lovely group.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: We try. She's done so much for the church. She ran the bake sale for thirty years.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. A legend.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She makes a lemon bar you would not believe.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'd like to have the recipe.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Oh, she'll never give it up. She'll take it to the grave.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Well, Hester, thank you for calling and for looking out for her.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Of course. I'll wait for your call.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Talk soon.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thank you. Bye bye.

Nurse -> Larkspur Home Health, this is Wendell.
Caller -> Hi, Wendell. This is Briony Castellanos. I'm calling about my grandfather. Anselm Castellanos.
Nurse -> Hi, Briony. How can I help?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm on my lunch break, so I'm eating a salad and calling.
Nurse -> No problem. Chew first.
Caller -> Ha. Okay.
Caller -> He forgot to take his pill this morning. The predisone. And it's two in the afternoon. I don't know if he should take it now.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me make sure I have the right one. Predisone, is that what it says on the bottle?
Caller -> That's how I say it. It's the steroid one. It's a little white pill. I'll read you the label. Hang on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> It says, um, predisone. Ten milligrams. Take one tablet by mouth every morning with food.
Nurse -> Got it. That sounds like his prednisone.
Nurse -> Is there a pharmacy name on the label?
Caller -> Yes. The one on Fifth. They're always so nice.
Caller -> Yes. That one.
Nurse -> When was his last dose?
Caller -> Yesterday morning. He took it with his oatmeal. Today he got up late, and he went straight to the garden. And I was at work. I'm here now on my break.
Nurse -> Okay. So he missed this morning.
Caller -> Yes. I came over at lunch, and I saw the pill still in the organizer.
Nurse -> Did you see him at lunch?
Caller -> I did. He's fine. He had a sandwich. He's been out in the yard moving rocks. At eighty five.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a lot of rocks.
Caller -> He's a lot of man.
Nurse -> Does he wear his hat out there, and drink water?
Caller -> The big straw hat. And I make him carry a bottle.
Nurse -> What's his date of birth, Briony?
Caller -> February second, nineteen thirty nine.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Two one two, five five five, zero one five six.
Nurse -> Perfect. How has he been feeling otherwise?
Caller -> Honestly? Kind of wired. He's been up at three in the morning the past few nights. Wandering the kitchen. Making toast. He's not tired but he's, like, buzzing.
Nurse -> That can be from the steroid. Is his appetite okay?
Caller -> Oh my gosh. He's eating everything. He ate a whole pie on Sunday. Not a slice. A pie.
Nurse -> Ha. Also a steroid effect.
Caller -> I figured. Is that normal?
Caller -> The pie, I thought we'd have to call you.
Nurse -> Ha. No emergency for a pie.
Nurse -> It's common. Any stomach pain, or heartburn? Black or dark stools?
Caller -> No. No stomach complaints. He'd tell me. And no, nothing dark. I help him in the bathroom sometimes.
Nurse -> Good. Okay, here's what to do. Give him the ten milligram tablet now, with some food. A sandwich or yogurt, something in his stomach. Then tomorrow morning give his regular dose as usual. Don't double up. And don't ever stop it suddenly.
Caller -> Give it now with food. Tomorrow regular. Don't double. Okay. He'll be annoyed. He thinks he doesn't need it.
Caller -> I'm writing it on a napkin. Napkin from the salad.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Ha. A lot of people feel that way. But the body gets used to it, so stopping fast can make him sick.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell him. I'll say the nurse said.
Nurse -> Say the nurse said. It works every time.
Caller -> Ha. Yes.
Nurse -> Give the pill in the morning, always. It's best early in the day, because later doses can keep him awake. The restlessness and the big appetite should ease when his dose goes down. Keep an eye on his stomach, and let us know if you see any pain or black stools.
Caller -> Morning. Watch his stomach. Black stools. Okay.
Nurse -> Could you set an alarm or put a sticky note on the organizer?
Caller -> I'll put a note on the coffee pot. He never misses the coffee.
Nurse -> That's a smart place.
Caller -> I'm full of ideas.
Nurse -> Does he live alone?
Caller -> With my grandmother. She's the one who takes his blood pressure every night. She's strict.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow morning to see how the night went and how he's feeling.
Caller -> That's great. I'll be at my desk. Call my cell. I'll pick up.
Caller -> Is nine okay? I have a meeting at ten.
Nurse -> Nine is fine. I'll call at nine.
Nurse -> Will do. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Oh, can he have coffee in the afternoon? He wants a cup.
Nurse -> Maybe decaf. Too much caffeine on top of the steroid won't help his sleep.
Caller -> Decaf. He'll complain. Okay.
Nurse -> Ha. Let him complain.
Caller -> I should go, my break's almost over.
Nurse -> Go ahead. One last thing, did he take anything else today?
Caller -> Just his water pill and the vitamin. I checked the organizer.
Caller -> Thank you, Wendell. I feel better.
Nurse -> Anytime. Bye, Briony.
Caller -> Bye.

turns.speaker: Nurse

turns.text: And a number for you?

turns.speaker: Caller

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. How has he been feeling otherwise?

turns.speaker: Caller

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That can be from the steroid. Is his appetite okay?

turns.speaker: Caller

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Also a steroid effect.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I figured. Is that normal?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The pie, I thought we'd have to call you.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. No emergency for a pie.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's common. Any stomach pain, or heartburn? Black or dark stools?

turns.speaker: Caller

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Okay, here's what to do. Give him the ten milligram tablet now, with some food. A sandwich or yogurt, something in his stomach. Then tomorrow morning give his regular dose as usual. Don't double up. And don't ever stop it suddenly.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Give it now with food. Tomorrow regular. Don't double. Okay. He'll be annoyed. He thinks he doesn't need it.

turns.speaker: Caller

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. A lot of people feel that way. But the body gets used to it, so stopping fast can make him sick.

turns.speaker: Caller

turns.speaker: Nurse

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Ha. Yes.

Nurse -> Meridian Home Health, this is Roxanne.
Caller -> Hi. Um. I saw something online. A job. For a, a nursing assistant. Is that still open?
Nurse -> I'm on the clinical line. I don't handle hiring. Which posting did you see?
Caller -> It was on one of those job sites. It said home health aide, nursing assistant, part time or full time. Evenings.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like one of ours. You'll want to apply through the careers page on our website.
Caller -> Okay. Can I just ask a couple of things first? Because I don't have the certificate yet.
Nurse -> Which certificate?
Caller -> The CNA. I'm in the class. I finish in March. But I have a lot of experience. I took care of my grandmother for three years.
Nurse -> That's great experience. I can't speak to the requirements. Human resources can tell you if you can start before you're certified.
Caller -> Do you know, like, what it pays?
Nurse -> I don't. It's not something I'm able to quote on this line.
Caller -> Okay. That's fair. Is there a number for human resources?
Nurse -> The number is on the website, under careers. They're open weekdays, eight to five.
Caller -> Weekdays eight to five. Okay. I'll look.
Nurse -> You can also leave your information with them and they'll call you back.
Caller -> Do they, like, drug test? Because I'm not worried, I just wanted to know.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, I don't have those details. HR will walk you through the whole process.
Caller -> Okay. Thanks. I'm sorry for bothering you. I didn't know who else to call.
Nurse -> It's no bother. Good luck with your class.
Caller -> Thanks. It's a lot of studying. Vital signs. Infection control. My brain hurts.
Nurse -> Ha. It gets easier. You'll do great.
Caller -> Thank you. Have a good day.
Nurse -> You too. Bye.

turns.text: I do. It's on him. It says, hold on, eighty six. Eighty six percent.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Is that bad? That's bad, right?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's lower than we want. That's why we're calling for help.

turns.text: Priya, I want you to call nine one one right now. Hang up with me and call. Or have someone else call while you stay with him.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay, okay, I'll yell for Marcus. Marcus! Call nine one one! Rosendo's choking! Sorry. He's going.

turns.speaker: Caller

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yes. He's on the desk phone. Okay.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Sit Rosendo straight up. Lean him a little forward. Don't lay him back.

turns.text: He's upright. I'm holding him. He's still coughing. He's coughing hard.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Is it okay to rub his back?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Not yet. Just hold him steady.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's good. Coughing means air is moving. Let him cough. Don't pat his back unless he stops coughing and can't breathe.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. He's coughing. It's getting a little clearer. A little.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Do not give him anything by mouth. No water, no food. Nothing.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Not even a sip? His mouth is dry.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Not even a sip. The paramedics will decide.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Nothing. Right. No water.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now and let them know.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Please.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: What's his date of birth, Priya? For the paramedics.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Um. April seventeenth, nineteen thirty two.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: April seventeenth, nineteen thirty two. Does he have any allergies, any DNR?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Not that I know. Penicillin maybe. I'll check.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I don't, hold on. He has a full code. I think. It's in the front of the chart. Marcus will have it. Marcus, grab Rosendo's chart!

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Keep him upright. Stay with him.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm here. I'm right here. His color's a little better. It's pink. It was blue.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Check the monitor again.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Hold on, it's jumping around because he's moving. It's, ninety one. Ninety one.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. Keep the finger still if you can.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Ninety one. It's coming up. Ninety one.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. That's improving. But he still needs to go to the hospital. The paramedics will check him.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yes. They're coming. Marcus says five minutes.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. What number are you calling from?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's the nurses' station. Five oh five, five five five, zero one five three.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Got it. Is there a family member to call?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: His son lives across town. He visits Sundays. Rosendo has a whole picture wall of grandchildren.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: His son. Marcus has the number. We'll call him once the ambulance is here.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Priya, you're doing great.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm so scared. He's like my grandpa. He tells me jokes every morning.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Stay calm. Talk to him. Tell him help is on the way.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He likes when I sing. I'll hum something. Sorry, this is silly.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's not silly. Anything that keeps him calm.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Rosendo, help's coming. You're okay. He's nodding. He squeezed my hand.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's good. Keep him calm and upright.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: They're asking me questions. What do I say?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Tell them what you told me. Coughing at lunch, pureed chicken, blue lips, eighty six percent, now ninety one.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Coughing, chicken, blue, eighty six, ninety one.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I hear the siren. They're here! They're here. Marcus is letting them in.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Marcus is getting his medication list too. The one with the heart pills.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Tell the paramedics what happened, and give them his chart. They'll take it from here.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Thank you. I have to go. Thank you!

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Bye!

Caller -> He's, he's okay. I think. He's hurting. And I can't figure out the morphine. The measuring.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's take it one thing at a time. I'm here.
Caller -> Thank you. I've been staring at this bottle for twenty minutes. I'm sorry to call so late.
Nurse -> Never apologize. That's what the line is for.
Caller -> I keep thinking I'll wake him. The house is so quiet.
Nurse -> Speak softly. He'll hear your voice and feel safer.
Caller -> My brother usually does the medicines. He's on a flight. He's flying in tonight, he lands at seven. So tonight it's me. Alone with Dad.
Nurse -> Okay. You've got me. Let's go through it. Can you read me the label on the morphine bottle?
Caller -> Hang on. I'm turning the light on. Okay. It says morphine sulfate oral solution. Twenty milligrams per milliliter. And then it says, concentrate. In bold. And then the directions say, give point two five milliliters every two hours as needed for pain.
Nurse -> Okay. And do you remember what the dose is in milligrams?
Caller -> The paper from the nurse says five milligrams. Five milligrams every two hours as needed.
Nurse -> That matches. Point two five milliliters is five milligrams, because the bottle has twenty milligrams in every full milliliter.
Caller -> Okay. But I don't understand. Five milligrams or point two five? Which one do I give?
Nurse -> Both mean the same thing. Five milligrams is the dose. Point two five milliliters, or a quarter of a milliliter, is how much liquid that is.
Caller -> Oh. So the milliliters is the amount of liquid. And the milligrams is the amount of medicine.
Nurse -> Exactly right.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. I was thinking milligrams meant I had to measure five of something.
Nurse -> It's a common mix up. Do you have the little oral syringe?
Caller -> I have two. The ones with the purple tops. They have lines on the side. There's a one, and a point five, and a lot of little lines.
Nurse -> Those are the ones. Look at the syringe. Which line is a quarter of a milliliter?
Caller -> There's, hold on, there's a line between the zero and the point five. A little one in the middle. Is that it?
Nurse -> That's it. Halfway to the point five line. That's a quarter.
Caller -> Okay. Halfway. I see it.
Nurse -> Draw the liquid up until the top of the black plunger tip lines up with that line. Not the end of the plunger, the top edge of the black part.
Caller -> The black part. Okay. Okay. Hold on. I drew some up. It's a little past. It's past the line.
Nurse -> Push a tiny bit back into the bottle until it lines up.
Caller -> Okay. Pushing. Okay. It's on the line. I think. Can you see it? Sorry. That's a silly question.
Nurse -> Ha. I can't, but it sounds like you've got it. Check at eye level.
Caller -> Eye level. Yes. It's on the line.
Nurse -> Now, when did he last have a dose?
Caller -> Ten o'clock tonight. It was a long time ago. It's almost four. No, it's three forty. I looked at the clock.
Nurse -> Okay. That's well over two hours. So he can have the dose now.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Where do I put it? Do I put it in his mouth?
Nurse -> Yes. Squirt it slowly in the pocket between his cheek and his gum. Not straight to the back of the throat. A little at a time.
Caller -> Cheek and gum. Slowly. Okay. He's awake, so he can swallow.
Nurse -> Good. Tell me how he's doing. How bad is his pain right now?
Caller -> He says a six. I asked him. He mumbled six. He's grimacing when I move him.
Nurse -> Where is the pain?
Caller -> I wish I could take it for him.
Nurse -> I know. That's what love does.
Caller -> He taught me to ride a bike on this street. Now I'm learning how to do this.
Nurse -> You're learning fast. And you don't have to do it perfectly.
Caller -> His back. Down low. And his hip. It's the same place it always is.
Nurse -> Okay. Go ahead and give the dose, and I'll stay on the line.
Caller -> Okay. I'm giving it. Slowly. Okay. He swallowed. He's making a face.
Nurse -> It tastes bitter. That's normal.
Caller -> Should I give him a sip of water after?
Nurse -> A tiny sip is fine, to rinse his mouth.
Caller -> Yes. He said yuck. That's a good sign. He's got some spunk.
Nurse -> Ha. Absolutely. Write down the time and the amount. A quarter of a milliliter. Five milligrams.
Caller -> I have the log. It's three forty five. Quarter milliliter. Five milligrams. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. The pain should ease in about twenty to thirty minutes. How many syringes do you have left? You said two.
Caller -> Two. I think. Let me look. Yes. Two. The one I just used and a clean one.
Nurse -> Okay. Rinse the used one with warm water, let it air dry, and reuse it. And I'll order more. I'll send a pack of syringes with the nurse in the morning.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. I was worried about that.
Nurse -> No need to worry. I'll make sure.
Caller -> I'm so glad I called. I almost didn't. I thought I'd figure it out.
Caller -> I kept saying, it's just a measuring thing, I'm a grown woman.
Nurse -> And a tired one. It's three forty in the morning.
Caller -> Ha. True.
Nurse -> You did figure it out. You just needed someone to say yes.
Caller -> Ha. Yes.
Nurse -> Can I get his date of birth, Ruthanne? I want to make sure I'm in the right chart.
Caller -> October twenty sixth, nineteen forty.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number to reach you, in case I need to call back?
Caller -> Two one two, five five five, zero one eight five. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. Now, I'd like to ask a few more things while I have you. Has he had a bowel movement?
Caller -> No. Not for three days. Three. I'm counting. He strains and nothing comes.
Nurse -> Is he on anything for that?
Caller -> The senna. The eight point six milligram. Twice a day. He had it tonight with dinner. Or with his applesauce, I guess. He didn't eat dinner.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep giving the senna twice a day. Don't skip it. And tell the nurse about the constipation when she comes in the morning, so she can add something if it's needed.
Caller -> Senna twice a day. Tell the nurse. Okay.
Nurse -> Is he on any other medicine tonight? Anything we haven't talked about?
Caller -> Just the usual. The anti-nausea one at bedtime. He took it.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> You said he didn't eat dinner. What did he have today?
Caller -> Just sips. Water. A few spoons of applesauce, and he threw away the rest. A sip of ginger ale. That's all.
Nurse -> Okay. That's common with the constipation and the pain. Don't force him. Offer small sips if he wants. Are his lips and mouth dry?
Caller -> Yes. They're cracked. He keeps licking them.
Nurse -> Do you have the little pink mouth swabs?
Caller -> I do. In the comfort box. And the lip balm, the one that's not petroleum.
Nurse -> Perfect. Wet the swab with water and wipe the inside of his mouth and his lips. Then put a bit of balm on. Do it every hour or two. It feels good to him.
Caller -> Swab. Water. Lips. Balm. Every hour or two. Okay.
Nurse -> And turn him gently from side to side every couple of hours. A pillow behind his back.
Caller -> I'll do that. He likes the pillow shaped like a banana.
Nurse -> Is the bed rail up on the side he's turning toward?
Caller -> Yes. I keep both up. My brother showed me.
Nurse -> Ha. A banana pillow. That's perfect.
Caller -> My mother bought it. It's the only thing he'll sleep on.
Nurse -> Then use it. Is his breathing okay? Any gurgling or noisy breathing? Hard work to breathe?
Caller -> No. It's quiet. He's snoring a little, but that's him. It's the normal snoring.
Nurse -> Does he wake easily?
Caller -> When I say his name, yes. He opens his eyes and goes back.
Nurse -> Good. That's what I like to hear.
Caller -> He's lucky to have you all. Honestly. I don't know what we'd do.
Nurse -> Thank you. That's kind.
Caller -> Can I tell you something? My dad was a pharmacist. For forty years. And he can't tell me how to measure his own morphine.
Nurse -> Oh, that's an irony. Did he try to help?
Caller -> He said, in his sleep, something about milliliters. That's all I got.
Nurse -> Ha. Some habits are strong.
Caller -> I laughed. Then I cried.
Nurse -> That's allowed.
Caller -> Dad would hate me crying. He'd say, go count something.
Nurse -> Ha. Count the syringes, then.
Caller -> Two. Still two.
Caller -> I know. Okay. I'm better now.
Nurse -> Good. I'm sending a nurse to see him in the morning. She should be there around nine.
Caller -> Around nine. Okay. My brother will be there by then, I hope. He lands at seven. The airport's an hour away.
Nurse -> He'll make it. Tell him to take a car, not the train, if he's tired.
Caller -> I texted him. He said he'll sleep on the plane.
Nurse -> That works. She'll check the pain and the bowels, and bring the syringes.
Caller -> Good. Perfect. Thank you.
Nurse -> Ruthanne, one more thing. If his pain isn't better in an hour, or you're unsure about a dose at any point tonight, call us right back. Any hour. Don't wait.
Caller -> Any hour. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> The next dose can be given at five forty five if he needs it. Not before.
Caller -> Five forty five. I'll set my phone alarm.
Nurse -> Perfect. And write it all down. It helps the morning nurse.
Caller -> I'm writing. Quarter ml. Five mg. Three forty five.
Nurse -> Read me the whole line from your log, so I know it's right.
Caller -> Three forty five. Morphine. Quarter milliliter. Five milligrams. By mouth.
Nurse -> That's perfect.
Nurse -> Beautiful. How is he now?
Caller -> He's calmer. He's lying back. His face looks softer. I think it's starting to work.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Stay close to him. Hold his hand if he wants.
Caller -> I'm going to sit on the bed. Is that okay? I won't bump him.
Nurse -> Sit by his good side. Slowly. That's fine.
Caller -> I am. He's holding mine. He squeezed it.
Caller -> You know, he hasn't done that in two days.
Nurse -> Then the pain is easing. Stay with him.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Anything else I can help with tonight?
Caller -> Should I wake him for his bedtime pills?
Nurse -> No. He's had them. Let him rest unless he wakes on his own.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let him sleep.
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Thank you so much, Genevieve. I really mean it.
Nurse -> You're doing a beautiful job. Call if you need anything.
Caller -> I will. Goodnight.
Nurse -> Goodnight, Ruthanne.

turns.text: Ha. A banana pillow. That's perfect.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: My mother bought it. It's the only thing he'll sleep on.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Then use it. Is his breathing okay? Any gurgling or noisy breathing? Hard work to breathe?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. It's quiet. He's snoring a little, but that's him. It's the normal snoring.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does he wake easily?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: When I say his name, yes. He opens his eyes and goes back.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. That's what I like to hear.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's lucky to have you all. Honestly. I don't know what we'd do.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Thank you. That's kind.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Can I tell you something? My dad was a pharmacist. For forty years. And he can't tell me how to measure his own morphine.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Oh, that's an irony. Did he try to help?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He said, in his sleep, something about milliliters. That's all I got.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Some habits are strong.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I laughed. Then I cried.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's allowed.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Dad would hate me crying. He'd say, go count something.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Count the syringes, then.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Two. Still two.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I know. Okay. I'm better now.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. I'm sending a nurse to see him in the morning. She should be there around nine.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Around nine. Okay. My brother will be there by then, I hope. He lands at seven. The airport's an hour away.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: He'll make it. Tell him to take a car, not the train, if he's tired.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I texted him. He said he'll sleep on the plane.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That works. She'll check the pain and the bowels, and bring the syringes.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Good. Perfect. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ruthanne, one more thing. If his pain isn't better in an hour, or you're unsure about a dose at any point tonight, call us right back. Any hour. Don't wait.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Any hour. Okay. I will.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The next dose can be given at five forty five if he needs it. Not before.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Five forty five. I'll set my phone alarm.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. And write it all down. It helps the morning nurse.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm writing. Quarter ml. Five mg. Three forty five.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Read me the whole line from your log, so I know it's right.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Three forty five. Morphine. Quarter milliliter. Five milligrams. By mouth.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's perfect.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Beautiful. How is he now?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's calmer. He's lying back. His face looks softer. I think it's starting to work.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's wonderful. Stay close to him. Hold his hand if he wants.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm going to sit on the bed. Is that okay? I won't bump him.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Sit by his good side. Slowly. That's fine.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I am. He's holding mine. He squeezed it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: You know, he hasn't done that in two days.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Then the pain is easing. Stay with him.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's a good sign. Anything else I can help with tonight?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Should I wake him for his bedtime pills?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: No. He's had them. Let him rest unless he wakes on his own.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I'll let him sleep.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. I think that's it. Thank you so much, Genevieve. I really mean it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You're doing a beautiful job. Call if you need anything.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I will. Goodnight.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Goodnight, Ruthanne.

Nurse -> Willowbrook Home Health, this is Fabian.
