Nurse -> Hi, Cordelia. I'm sorry to hear that. Margarita, is she with you?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little frazzled. I haven't had coffee yet and it's two in the afternoon.
Nurse -> Take a breath. I'm listening.
Caller -> She's at her house. I'm there now. I came over at lunch because she didn't answer her phone.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the confusion.
Caller -> She woke up this way. She thinks it's Tuesday. She keeps asking where my father is. He passed twelve years ago.
Nurse -> Does she know who you are?
Caller -> Yes, she knows me. She just thinks I'm there to help with the garden.
Nurse -> That's new for Margarita?
Caller -> Brand new. She's sharp. She does the crossword in pen. This morning she called me the wrong name and didn't know she'd done it.
Nurse -> Has anything changed lately? New medicine, a new place, anything stressful?
Caller -> Nothing new. Same pills. Same routine. The only thing was the cold snap last week and she wouldn't turn up the heat.
Nurse -> Ha. Confident.
Caller -> She's never been wrong about a word in her life. Until today. She wrote a seven letter word in a four letter box.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she had any fever?
Caller -> I took it. It was a hundred point two. I used the ear one.
Nurse -> Was it in both ears or one?
Caller -> I did both. Hundred point two and a hundred point one. So about the same.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> A hundred point two. Okay. Any other symptoms? Pain when she urinates? Changes in the urine?
Caller -> She hasn't said anything about pain. But I went in the bathroom and the smell. It was strong. Really strong. And dark.
Nurse -> Any blood that you could see?
Caller -> No. Just dark, like tea.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she had urinary infections before?
Caller -> Twice. Last year and the year before. Both times it started with the confusion. Before the burning, before anything. The doctor said that's how it goes with her age.
Nurse -> That's right. It's very common in older adults.
Caller -> I wish someone had told me the first time.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Is she drinking?
Caller -> Hardly. I put out a glass of water and a cup of tea this morning and neither one was touched. She had maybe a few sips of juice.
Nurse -> Has she been to the bathroom today, as far as you know?
Caller -> I don't think so. I didn't see her go. I came at noon and the toilet hadn't been flushed since the morning.
Caller -> I tried a straw. She waved it away.
Nurse -> Sometimes a straw is easier. Or a spoon.
Nurse -> Did she fall? Hit her head? Any bruises?
Caller -> No. No falls. I looked her over. No bruises. She's been in her chair. I checked her walker and it's right where it should be.
Caller -> And the stairs are fine. She hasn't gone near them.
Nurse -> Good. And can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> May thirtieth, nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number for you?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, zero one two nine.
Nurse -> Got it. Cordelia, how is her breathing?
Caller -> Normal. She's not short of breath. Her color is okay.
Nurse -> Any chest pain, cough?
Caller -> No cough. She'd tell me if her chest hurt. She complains about everything else.
Nurse -> Ha. Good.
Nurse -> Is she able to swallow and take her pills?
Caller -> I haven't tried the pills. I didn't want to give her anything without asking.
Nurse -> That's wise. Let's hold her morning pills until the clinician calls. She hasn't had any Tylenol?
Caller -> No. Nothing. I wasn't sure about the Tylenol.
Nurse -> Wait for the clinician on that, too.
Caller -> Okay. I'll wait.
Nurse -> I'll tell the clinician you're holding them.
Caller -> Thank you. I wasn't sure what was safe.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician now, and I'll tell them what you told me. Confusion, a hundred point two, strong urine, and hardly drinking.
Caller -> Please. Thank you. I'm so scared it's the same as last time. She ended up in the hospital for a week.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll try to catch it early. I'm also scheduling a nurse to visit this afternoon.
Caller -> This afternoon. What time?
Caller -> I need to move my mother's cat off the chair so the nurse can sit.
Nurse -> Ha. Good luck with that.
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a window. It'll probably be between two and four.
Caller -> I'll be here. I took the day off.
Caller -> I work at the post office. They were fine. They said family first.
Nurse -> Good for them.
Nurse -> Good. In the meantime, let's get some fluids into her. Offer small sips of water or juice every fifteen minutes. Don't force it, but keep offering. And keep track of what she drinks, and when she last went to the bathroom.
Caller -> Small sips every fifteen minutes. Write down what she drinks. Write down the bathroom. Okay. I have a pen.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Should I take her to the emergency room?
Nurse -> Not right now. Let the clinician decide. They'll call you back shortly. If anything changes, we'll reconsider.
Caller -> Okay. What would change it?
Nurse -> If she can't be woken up, if she has a seizure, or if she has trouble breathing, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Can't wake her. Seizure. Trouble breathing. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else you notice, call us.
Caller -> I will. She's resting now. She's dozing in the chair.
Nurse -> Let her rest. But if she's sleeping a lot, try to wake her for sips.
Caller -> She sleeps most of the afternoon anyway. How do I tell the difference?
Nurse -> If she wakes easily to her name and can sip, that's okay. If she's hard to wake or won't respond, call us right away.
Caller -> Okay. Easy to wake is okay. Hard to wake is not.
Caller -> I will. Her cat's on her lap. It's the only thing keeping her calm.
Nurse -> Ha. A good nurse.
Caller -> He doesn't leave her side. He sleeps on her feet at night.
Caller -> The best. Winston. He's a big orange thing.
Nurse -> Does she have her glasses nearby?
Caller -> She's wearing them on top of her head like a headband.
Caller -> Yes. On her head. Where she always loses them.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course.
Caller -> Do you want me to keep the phone line open for the clinician?
Nurse -> Yes. Keep your cell near you. They'll call within fifteen minutes.
Caller -> Should I call my brother too? He's in Denver.
Nurse -> Yes, let him know. Family should be aware, especially if she goes to the hospital.
Caller -> I'll call him after we hang up. He'll want to fly out.
Caller -> Okay. I'll keep it in my hand.
Nurse -> Thank you, Cordelia. We'll take good care of Margarita.
Caller -> Fabian, do you think it's a urinary infection again?
Nurse -> It could be. The clinician and the nurse will check. I don't want to guess over the phone.
Caller -> That's fair. I just want to be ready.
Caller -> It's Marguerite, but that's okay. She'd laugh.
Nurse -> Oh, I'm sorry. Marguerite.
Caller -> No worries. Everyone gets it wrong.
Caller -> It's spelled M A R G U E R I T E. French. Her mother was from Quebec.
Nurse -> Beautiful name. I'll make sure the chart has it spelled that way.
Nurse -> I'll fix it in the chart.
Caller -> One more thing, can I use the bathroom while she's dozing, or should I stay right here?
Nurse -> Go ahead, but keep the door open and listen for her.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you for putting up with me.
Nurse -> You're doing a great job.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cypress Home Health, this is Lorenzo.
Caller -> Hi, Lorenzo. It's Lorraine Dufresne. I'm a patient of yours. I have the colostomy. I'm running low on stuff and I've got a skin problem too.
Nurse -> Hi, Lorraine. Okay. Let's start with the supplies. What are you running low on?
Caller -> The wafers. The skin barriers. I have three left. And I'm out of the paste. The little tube. I used the last of it Wednesday.
Nurse -> Three wafers. And no paste.
Caller -> Right. And I'm going through them faster because the bag keeps leaking. I'm changing it every day, and it's supposed to be every three or four.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the skin issue you mentioned?
Caller -> Yes. The skin around the stoma is red. It's kind of irritated. It's like a ring. It burns when I change the bag. It's about this big, around the whole thing.
Nurse -> Is it open? Any weeping, or blisters, or pus?
Caller -> I appreciate you being patient with me.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> No. It's just red. No pus. No yellow. It's not open. It's like a sunburn.
Nurse -> And any fever?
Caller -> Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> No. I feel fine. I take my temperature every morning because I'm paranoid. It's been normal.
Nurse -> Ha. A little paranoia is good. What's your output like?
Caller -> Normal. Regular. Soft. Twice a day. No change.
Nurse -> Good. Date of birth, Lorraine?
Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Caller -> January thirteenth, nineteen sixty eight.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one one zero.
Nurse -> Perfect. So here's what I'm going to do. I'll order the wafers, a couple of tubes of paste, and a barrier powder to help the skin.
Caller -> Oh, the powder. Yes. My last nurse used it. I don't have any.
Nurse -> That's what the redness needs. I'll also send a nurse to see how the pouch is fitting and look at the skin. She'll come Tuesday.
Caller -> Tuesday. Okay. Is there anything I can do until then?
Nurse -> Yes. When the pouch leaks, change it right away. Don't leave it on. Clean the skin with plain warm water, no soap, no wipes with alcohol. Pat it all the way dry. If you have any powder or a cream from before, use just a little before the new wafer.
Caller -> Plain water. Dry it all the way. Powder. I don't have any powder. I'll just do water and dry it.
Nurse -> That's fine. Make sure the wafer opening is cut right. Not too big. Just a little bigger than the stoma.
Caller -> I trace it. I use the little template.
Nurse -> Perfect. And with only three wafers, change only when it leaks, not on a schedule.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Okay. I'll stretch them.

turns.text: Good idea. I'll pause.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I'll be here. I work from home on Wednesdays.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: In the meantime, weigh yourself every morning. After you use the bathroom, before you eat, same scale, same clothes. Write it down. If you gain more than two pounds in a day, or five pounds in a week, call us.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Every morning. Same scale. Write it down. Two in a day, five in a week. Okay. I have a log. It's on the fridge.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Great. Now the food. Keep your salt low. That means skipping the pizza, canned soup, deli meat, chips. And keep your fluids to what the doctor told you.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Low salt. No pizza. I know. I'll go back to the plan.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Don't beat yourself up. One weekend. Just get back on track.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. I'm usually good. My wife keeps me honest.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. A good wife.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha, no worries.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The best. She's hiding the chips.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Anders, if you get chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or you faint, call nine one one. Don't wait.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Chest pain. Bad breathing. Fainting. Nine one one. Okay.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Any questions?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Of course.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Just one. Can I still walk? I walk the dog every morning. Should I stop?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Short, slow walks are fine. Stop if you get winded or dizzy.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Take your time, there's no rush.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Slow. He pulls, but I'll hold him.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: What kind of dog?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sorry, I lost my train of thought.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's okay. We were just getting started.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A beagle. He's a menace.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Beagles are.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: No problem, I'll hold.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He ate a sock last week. We had a whole vet visit.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Oh no. Is he okay?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Let me grab my glasses, one second.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Sure, I'll wait.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's fine. The sock was not.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Good.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Can you hear me okay? The signal's a little weak.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I can hear you fine.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thanks, Ansgar.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You're welcome. Take care, Anders.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Home Health, this is Magdalena.
Caller -> Hi, Magdalena. It's Berenice Dunmore. I'm calling about my husband, Hollis Dunmore. I need to order supplies for his tube feeding.
Nurse -> Hi, Berenice. I can help. Let's go through what you have. What are you running low on?
Caller -> Everything, honestly. I should have called last week. I've been so busy.
Nurse -> Busy with Hollis?
Caller -> With Hollis, with the house, with my daughter's wedding in the spring. I keep forgetting what day it is.
Nurse -> That's what lists are for. We'll build one.
Nurse -> That's all right. We'll go item by item. Start with the formula. How many cans?
Caller -> I have four. Four cans of the formula. The Jevity. It's what he takes. Four left in the cupboard.
Nurse -> Is the cupboard cool and dry? Not near the stove?
Caller -> It's the bottom shelf in the pantry. Dark and cool. I rotate them, oldest in front.
Nurse -> You're better organized than you think.
Nurse -> And how many does he use in a day?
Caller -> Five. He gets five cans a day. So four is, what, less than a day.
Nurse -> It's under a day. We'll make sure it comes soon. What about the feeding bags?
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> I have two. I wash them. The nurse said I can reuse them for a few days. But I'm on the last two.
Nurse -> Okay. And the extension set? The little tube that connects to the button?
Caller -> One. I have one. The other one cracked. I threw it out.
Nurse -> Okay. And the syringes? The sixty milliliter ones for flushing.
Caller -> One syringe. It's the only one. The plunger sticks. It's been sticking for a week.
Nurse -> Is it the rubber part that sticks, or the whole thing?
Caller -> The rubber part. It drags and I have to push hard. I'm afraid I'll push too hard and it'll pop off.
Nurse -> Don't force it. Stop using it if it drags. Is there any other syringe in the house?
Caller -> A smaller one, from the pharmacy. For the pills.
Nurse -> Use that for medicines only, and I'll get you proper flushing syringes.
Nurse -> That one needs replacing, too. How about the gauze for around the tube site?
Caller -> Almost out. I have maybe two pieces. The little split ones. I've been cutting regular gauze to fit.
Nurse -> That can leave loose threads near the opening, so I'd stop.
Caller -> I see. I didn't know. I thought it was the same.
Nurse -> Okay. Don't cut the regular gauze. We'll send the split ones.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Let's ask about the site. How does it look?
Caller -> It's, there's a little pink bit of skin around the hole. Pink, like a raised bit. It doesn't hurt him. It doesn't bleed.
Nurse -> Any drainage? Any leaking from around the tube?
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> No. It's dry. Clean. No smell.
Nurse -> Any fever? Vomiting?
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> No. No fever. No throwing up. He tolerates the feeds. He's very good.
Nurse -> How long does each feeding take?
Caller -> About an hour. He sits up the whole time in the recliner. I make him stay upright for another hour after.
Nurse -> Exactly right.
Nurse -> Good. That pink tissue is probably granulation tissue. A nurse will look at it. Can I have his date of birth?
Caller -> March third, nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, zero one nine zero.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to order the formula, the feeding bags, extension sets, syringes, and the split gauze. I'll order extras of each so you don't run low again.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. That would help. I'd love not to think about it for a few weeks.
Nurse -> We'll have it delivered Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. That's, what's today? Wednesday. So tomorrow. Okay. Good. I'll be home all day.
Nurse -> Does the delivery driver need to ring, or is there a gate?
Caller -> No gate. Just ring the bell twice. Hollis can't hear it, but the dog can.
Nurse -> Four cans won't last until tomorrow. How are you going to cover tonight and tomorrow morning?
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> I have a few cartons of the other kind. The vanilla. From the hospital. I could give that.
Nurse -> Is that the same formula?
Caller -> No. The hospital gave us a different one. A shake. But he's had it.
Nurse -> I'd rather not switch without asking. Let me check with the dietitian, or have the nurse call you back tonight. In the meantime, the four cans should cover this evening and tomorrow's early feeds.
Caller -> Okay. I'll stretch it. I'll do the last can in the morning.
Nurse -> And to be clear, the dietitian or the nurse will call you tonight if there's anything to change.
Caller -> Tonight. Okay. I'll answer the phone even if it's a number I don't know.
Caller -> Is it okay if I dilute it a little, to make it last?
Nurse -> No, please don't dilute it. Give him the usual amount. Ask me if you're short.
Caller -> Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> Good. If you're short, call me back, and I'll arrange something.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. I feel better already.
Nurse -> Berenice, you mentioned a question about flushing. What was that?
Caller -> Yes. I don't remember how often to flush. The paper said before and after but I do it only after. I think. Am I doing it wrong?
Nurse -> Let's go over it. You flush with sixty milliliters of water before every feeding, and again after. And before and after any medicine. That keeps the tube from clogging.
Caller -> Before and after. Sixty. Each time. And the medicines too. Oh, I've been missing the before.
Nurse -> That's okay. Start doing both from now on. And wash the syringe and the bag in warm soapy water after each use. Let them air dry.
Caller -> Warm soapy water. Air dry. I do that already. I put them on a towel by the window.
Caller -> Sometimes I forget and the bag sits in the sink overnight. Is that bad?
Nurse -> Rinse it well in the morning and wash it again. If it smells, throw it away.
Caller -> Smell test. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now for the tube site. Clean around it once a day with warm water, no peroxide, no alcohol. Pat it dry and put a clean split gauze under the tube.
Caller -> Warm water. Dry. Split gauze. Okay. I'll stop cutting the other kind.
Nurse -> Yes. Use the split ones as soon as they arrive. Berenice, call us if you see drainage or the redness spreading, a fever, vomiting, if the tube clogs and won't clear, or if the tube comes out.
Caller -> Drainage. Redness. Fever. Vomiting. Clog. Tube out. I'm writing it. I have the list from before. I'll add the clog part.
Nurse -> If the tube comes out, that's urgent. The hole can start to close in an hour or two. Call right away.
Caller -> Okay. Right away. I'll put the number on the fridge. Again.
Caller -> The magnet fell off. I keep sticking it back on.
Nurse -> Ha. Try the freezer door. Magnets love the freezer.
Caller -> Ha. I'll move it.
Nurse -> Good. I'll also send a nurse on Friday to look at the site and watch you do a flush, so we can be sure it's right.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. Is that in the morning?
Nurse -> Probably. The scheduler will call you.
Caller -> Should I have him ready, or dressed, or anything?
Nurse -> Just as he is. Maybe have his chair clear so she can reach the tube. She'll want to see the site in good light.
Caller -> I'll open the curtains.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> I'll be here. Hollis gets up late, so any time is fine.
Nurse -> Perfect. How is he doing otherwise? Is he comfortable?
Caller -> He's good. He's in his chair watching the football. He's yelling at the screen. It's his team.
Nurse -> Does he talk back to the referees?
Caller -> He does. In full sentences. He taught the dog to bark at fumbles.
Nurse -> Ha. I love that.
Nurse -> Ha. Who's he rooting for?
Caller -> The Titans. He's been a fan since before they were the Titans. When they were the Oilers.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a long time.
Caller -> Fifty years. He's got the jersey. It doesn't fit him anymore.
Nurse -> Ha. But he wears it anyway.
Caller -> Every Sunday. Over his pajamas.
Nurse -> That's wonderful.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> It's the little things. I'm learning that.
Nurse -> How are you doing, Berenice? It's a lot to manage.
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm tired. I do everything. The feeds, the flushes, the laundry. But I wouldn't have it any other way. I just want him home.
Nurse -> He's lucky to have you.
Caller -> I'm lucky to have him. Fifty one years in March. He proposed at a bowling alley.
Nurse -> A bowling alley! Did he roll a strike?
Caller -> A gutter ball. He says that's why I said yes. I felt sorry for him.
Nurse -> Ha. A wonderful story.
Nurse -> You're doing a beautiful job. Do you have help? Family, friends?
Caller -> I also have a church group. They offered to sit with Hollis so I can go to the store.
Nurse -> Take them up on it. You deserve an hour to yourself.
Caller -> My son comes Saturdays. And a neighbor brings casseroles. I can't eat that many casseroles.
Nurse -> Ha. Freeze a few.
Caller -> I have. The freezer is full of casseroles.
Nurse -> Any chance of a tuna one? Just kidding.
Caller -> I'll bring you one. They're all macaroni, I think.
Nurse -> Ha. You're sweet.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good problem.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.
Nurse -> That's completely understandable.
Caller -> It's a blessing, I know. I shouldn't complain.
Nurse -> It's okay to be tired. Please tell the nurse on Friday if you need more help. We have resources.
Caller -> Thank you for saying that. Nobody asks me how I'm doing. They all ask how Hollis is.
Nurse -> That happens to caregivers all the time. You matter in this too.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. That means a lot.
Nurse -> Anytime. Is there anything else you need today?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Oh, the tape. Do you send tape?
Nurse -> We'll add the paper tape to the order.
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> Perfect. Thank you.
Caller -> I can't thank you enough. Truly. Before you all came, I was doing this alone with a binder from the hospital.
Nurse -> You were doing it well. We just fill in the gaps.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care, Berenice.
Caller -> You too. Bye now.

turns.text: I have four. Four cans of the formula. The Jevity. It's what he takes. Four left in the cupboard.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is the cupboard cool and dry? Not near the stove?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's the bottom shelf in the pantry. Dark and cool. I rotate them, oldest in front.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You're better organized than you think.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: And how many does he use in a day?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Five. He gets five cans a day. So four is, what, less than a day.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's under a day. We'll make sure it comes soon. What about the feeding bags?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sorry, I just dropped my pen.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's all right.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I have two. I wash them. The nurse said I can reuse them for a few days. But I'm on the last two.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. And the extension set? The little tube that connects to the button?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: One. I have one. The other one cracked. I threw it out.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. And the syringes? The sixty milliliter ones for flushing.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: One syringe. It's the only one. The plunger sticks. It's been sticking for a week.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is it the rubber part that sticks, or the whole thing?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The rubber part. It drags and I have to push hard. I'm afraid I'll push too hard and it'll pop off.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Don't force it. Stop using it if it drags. Is there any other syringe in the house?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A smaller one, from the pharmacy. For the pills.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Use that for medicines only, and I'll get you proper flushing syringes.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That one needs replacing, too. How about the gauze for around the tube site?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Almost out. I have maybe two pieces. The little split ones. I've been cutting regular gauze to fit.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That can leave loose threads near the opening, so I'd stop.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I see. I didn't know. I thought it was the same.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. Don't cut the regular gauze. We'll send the split ones.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Let's ask about the site. How does it look?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's, there's a little pink bit of skin around the hole. Pink, like a raised bit. It doesn't hurt him. It doesn't bleed.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Any drainage? Any leaking from around the tube?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Let me grab my glasses, one second.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Sure, I'll wait.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. It's dry. Clean. No smell.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Any fever? Vomiting?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: No problem, take your time.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. No fever. No throwing up. He tolerates the feeds. He's very good.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: How long does each feeding take?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: About an hour. He sits up the whole time in the recliner. I make him stay upright for another hour after.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Exactly right.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. That pink tissue is probably granulation tissue. A nurse will look at it. Can I have his date of birth?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: March third, nineteen fifty one.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: And a number for you?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Six one five, five five five, zero one nine zero.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Got it. I'm going to order the formula, the feeding bags, extension sets, syringes, and the split gauze. I'll order extras of each so you don't run low again.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Oh, thank you. That would help. I'd love not to think about it for a few weeks.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: We'll have it delivered Thursday.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thursday. That's, what's today? Wednesday. So tomorrow. Okay. Good. I'll be home all day.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does the delivery driver need to ring, or is there a gate?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No gate. Just ring the bell twice. Hollis can't hear it, but the dog can.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Four cans won't last until tomorrow. How are you going to cover tonight and tomorrow morning?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Alright, thank you.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I have a few cartons of the other kind. The vanilla. From the hospital. I could give that.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is that the same formula?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. The hospital gave us a different one. A shake. But he's had it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'd rather not switch without asking. Let me check with the dietitian, or have the nurse call you back tonight. In the meantime, the four cans should cover this evening and tomorrow's early feeds.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I'll stretch it. I'll do the last can in the morning.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: And to be clear, the dietitian or the nurse will call you tonight if there's anything to change.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Tonight. Okay. I'll answer the phone even if it's a number I don't know.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Is it okay if I dilute it a little, to make it last?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: No, please don't dilute it. Give him the usual amount. Ask me if you're short.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I won't.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. If you're short, call me back, and I'll arrange something.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I will. Thank you. I feel better already.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Berenice, you mentioned a question about flushing. What was that?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yes. I don't remember how often to flush. The paper said before and after but I do it only after. I think. Am I doing it wrong?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Let's go over it. You flush with sixty milliliters of water before every feeding, and again after. And before and after any medicine. That keeps the tube from clogging.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Before and after. Sixty. Each time. And the medicines too. Oh, I've been missing the before.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's okay. Start doing both from now on. And wash the syringe and the bag in warm soapy water after each use. Let them air dry.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Warm soapy water. Air dry. I do that already. I put them on a towel by the window.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sometimes I forget and the bag sits in the sink overnight. Is that bad?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Rinse it well in the morning and wash it again. If it smells, throw it away.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Smell test. Okay.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. Now for the tube site. Clean around it once a day with warm water, no peroxide, no alcohol. Pat it dry and put a clean split gauze under the tube.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Warm water. Dry. Split gauze. Okay. I'll stop cutting the other kind.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Yes. Use the split ones as soon as they arrive. Berenice, call us if you see drainage or the redness spreading, a fever, vomiting, if the tube clogs and won't clear, or if the tube comes out.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Drainage. Redness. Fever. Vomiting. Clog. Tube out. I'm writing it. I have the list from before. I'll add the clog part.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: If the tube comes out, that's urgent. The hole can start to close in an hour or two. Call right away.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Right away. I'll put the number on the fridge. Again.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The magnet fell off. I keep sticking it back on.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Try the freezer door. Magnets love the freezer.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Ha. I'll move it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. I'll also send a nurse on Friday to look at the site and watch you do a flush, so we can be sure it's right.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Friday. Okay. Is that in the morning?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Probably. The scheduler will call you.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Should I have him ready, or dressed, or anything?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Just as he is. Maybe have his chair clear so she can reach the tube. She'll want to see the site in good light.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll open the curtains.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha, no worries.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll be here. Hollis gets up late, so any time is fine.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. How is he doing otherwise? Is he comfortable?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's good. He's in his chair watching the football. He's yelling at the screen. It's his team.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does he talk back to the referees?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He does. In full sentences. He taught the dog to bark at fumbles.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. I love that.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Who's he rooting for?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The Titans. He's been a fan since before they were the Titans. When they were the Oilers.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. That's a long time.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Fifty years. He's got the jersey. It doesn't fit him anymore.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. But he wears it anyway.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Every Sunday. Over his pajamas.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's wonderful.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I understand. Take a breath.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's the little things. I'm learning that.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: How are you doing, Berenice? It's a lot to manage.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm okay. I'm tired. I do everything. The feeds, the flushes, the laundry. But I wouldn't have it any other way. I just want him home.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: He's lucky to have you.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm lucky to have him. Fifty one years in March. He proposed at a bowling alley.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: A bowling alley! Did he roll a strike?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A gutter ball. He says that's why I said yes. I felt sorry for him.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. A wonderful story.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You're doing a beautiful job. Do you have help? Family, friends?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I also have a church group. They offered to sit with Hollis so I can go to the store.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Take them up on it. You deserve an hour to yourself.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: My son comes Saturdays. And a neighbor brings casseroles. I can't eat that many casseroles.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Freeze a few.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I have. The freezer is full of casseroles.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Any chance of a tuna one? Just kidding.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll bring you one. They're all macaroni, I think.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. You're sweet.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. That's a good problem.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's completely understandable.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's a blessing, I know. I shouldn't complain.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's okay to be tired. Please tell the nurse on Friday if you need more help. We have resources.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thank you for saying that. Nobody asks me how I'm doing. They all ask how Hollis is.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That happens to caregivers all the time. You matter in this too.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I will. Thank you. That means a lot.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Anytime. Is there anything else you need today?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. I think that's it. Oh, the tape. Do you send tape?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: We'll add the paper tape to the order.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's fine.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Perfect. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I can't thank you enough. Truly. Before you all came, I was doing this alone with a binder from the hospital.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You were doing it well. We just fill in the gaps.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You're welcome. Take care, Berenice.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: You too. Bye now.

Caller -> No. No vomiting. He didn't pass out. I heard the thump and I ran in and he was awake. He was sitting up already.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep him still. Don't let him stand or walk around. Keep him lying down, or sitting against the wall if that's more comfortable. Don't move his neck.
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> He's against the wall. He wants to get up. I'm telling him no. Dad, stay. Stay put.
Nurse -> That's right. Give him nothing by mouth. No water, no food, no pills.

Nurse -> No. None of them. Especially not the warfarin. Don't give him any of his medicines until the doctors say so.
Caller -> No pills. Okay. I'm putting them away. Not yet. Hold on, I'm pressing. I can't. Okay. Greg's got the pills.
Nurse -> Good. Tell me when the dispatcher says they're on the way.
Caller -> Greg says they're sending an ambulance. They said ten minutes. Ten minutes.
Nurse -> Perfect. Stay with him. What's his date of birth, Annalise? For the paramedics.
Caller -> December fifteenth, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> And the best number to reach you?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one nine eight. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now so they know what's happening.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Please.
Nurse -> Is the bleeding slowing at all?
Caller -> I don't know. Hold on. I can't look. If I lift it, it'll start again. The towel's heavy.
Nurse -> Don't lift. Just keep the pressure steady.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> Okay. I'm leaning on it. He's wincing.
Nurse -> I know. It hurts, but it's important. Talk to him. Keep him awake. Ask him his name, where he lives.
Caller -> Dad, what's your name? Sylvester. Where do you live? Dad? He says Cedar Street. That's right. And he said the year. He said nineteen... no, he said the wrong year.
Nurse -> What year did he say?
Caller -> He said twenty ten. It's twenty twenty six.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that, too. He's confused about the date.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I will. I'll tell them everything.

Caller -> On the fridge. A printed list. Greg is grabbing it for them.

Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> No. I'm fine. I'm just scared. My hands are shaking. I'm covered in his blood.
Nurse -> That's okay. You're doing great. Wash up after they take over, and wear gloves if you have them.
Caller -> I'll wash. I don't have gloves.
Nurse -> It's fine. Keep going.
Caller -> I hear something outside. Is that the sirens? Hold on. Greg, is that them?
Nurse -> Take your time. I'm here.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Yes, yes, they're pulling up. Greg's going to the door. Okay. Here they come.
Nurse -> Good. Tell the paramedics the warfarin and the wrong date. They'll take it from here.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. Thank you, Valentina.
Nurse -> Go ahead. We'll follow up with the family.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sunrise Valley Home Health, this is Percival.
Caller -> Hi, Percival. It's Josephine Alderete. I'm one of your patients. I have diabetes. I'm calling for a regular check in and I need to ask about my appointment.
Nurse -> Hi, Josephine. Good to hear from you. Let me pull up your chart. Can I have your date of birth?
Caller -> February twentieth, nineteen sixty seven.
Nurse -> Perfect. And the best number to reach you?
Caller -> Six one zero, five five five, zero one five four.
Nurse -> Got it. How have you been feeling?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Honestly pretty good. Better than I have in a while. I wanted to tell somebody, so I'm telling you.
Nurse -> That's wonderful to hear. What do you think made the difference?
Caller -> A lot of little things. I'll get to it. Don't let me ramble.
Nurse -> Ramble away. I have time.
Nurse -> I'm glad. What's your morning glucose been running?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I've been writing it down every day. I add them up on Sundays. The average this week was one eighteen. Last week was one twenty five. Before that I was in the one forties.
Nurse -> That's a nice trend. Are you taking your metformin?
Caller -> The doctor said the number I want to see is the A1C, right? That's the three month one.
Nurse -> Right. That comes from a blood test. The next one is due soon, and we'll go over it Friday.
Caller -> Okay. I'm a little afraid to see it. But I think it will be better.
Nurse -> With these numbers, I'd expect an improvement.
Caller -> Yes. Five hundred milligrams. Twice a day. With breakfast and with dinner. I took it this morning.
Nurse -> Any stomach upset with it?
Caller -> A little at first. Not anymore. I take it with food like you said.
Caller -> I thought about stopping it because of that. Then I read you shouldn't stop without asking.
Nurse -> Exactly. Always call first. I'm glad you did not.
Caller -> I called your office and a nurse told me to take it with food. Same advice.
Nurse -> Good. Any other medicines?
Caller -> Just my blood pressure one and a baby aspirin. Nothing new.
Nurse -> Any over the counter things, vitamins, supplements, herbal teas?
Caller -> A multivitamin and chamomile tea at night. That's it. I Googled the tea and it said fine.
Nurse -> Chamomile is okay for most people. Mention it to the doctor.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> Any dizziness with the blood pressure one?
Caller -> No. It's been steady. I check it at the pharmacy on Saturdays. They have a machine.
Nurse -> Good habit.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you've changed. You said you're doing better.
Caller -> I'm walking. Twenty minutes every morning after breakfast. Around the neighborhood with my sister. And I stopped the soda. I was drinking three a day. Now it's sparkling water with lime.
Caller -> We go past the bakery, which is cruel. The smell is everything.
Nurse -> Ha. A test of willpower.
Caller -> I walk faster past it.
Nurse -> Any pain when you walk? Calf cramps, anything?
Caller -> No. A little tired in the last five minutes. That's all.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Three sodas a day is a big sugar load.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.
Nurse -> That's completely understandable.
Caller -> I know. I was embarrassed to tell the doctor. Now I'm proud of myself.
Nurse -> Doctors have heard it all. Honestly, they love when patients change something.
Caller -> That's what my sister said. She dragged me to the last visit.
Nurse -> Sisters are useful.
Caller -> She's very bossy. But she's right about eighty percent of the time.
Nurse -> You should be. Any symptoms? Thirst, urinating a lot?
Caller -> No. That's gone. I used to get up three times a night. Now once.
Nurse -> That's a good sign your sugars are steadier.
Caller -> I sleep better. I haven't had coffee after noon, either. My sister's rule.
Nurse -> Any problems with your feet? Numbness, burning, sores?
Caller -> The tingling. In my toes. Mostly the big toes. At night when I'm lying in bed. It's been there a few months. It's not painful. Just a pins and needles feeling.
Nurse -> Okay. Is that the same or worse than last time?
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> About the same. Maybe a tiny bit more when I'm tired.
Nurse -> Does it keep you from sleeping?
Caller -> No. I notice it, then I fall asleep. I put a pillow under my feet and it settles.
Nurse -> Good trick.
Nurse -> Any cuts, sores, blisters, or color changes on your feet?
Caller -> No. I look every night, like you told me. I use a mirror from the bathroom. They look fine. No sores. And my vision's fine. I got new glasses in the fall, but nothing's changed.
Nurse -> Good. Keep doing exactly that. Do you wear shoes and socks around the house?
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> Socks, yes. Shoes mostly. I have the soft slippers for the bedroom.
Nurse -> What kind of shoes? Closed toe, with room?
Caller -> Sneakers. A half size bigger, my sister made me. They're ugly but comfortable.
Nurse -> Ugly and comfortable is exactly what we want.
Nurse -> Good. Now, supplies. How are your test strips?
Caller -> Wait, before the strips, can I ask about Thanksgiving? It's coming up and I'm nervous.
Nurse -> Of course. What are you worried about?
Caller -> The pie. And my mother's stuffing. Everything is carbs. I don't want to ruin the progress.
Nurse -> One holiday meal won't undo it. Eat a normal plate, go for a walk after, and don't skip breakfast to save room.
Caller -> A walk after. My sister will love that. She wants everyone on a family walk.
Nurse -> It's a good tradition. Start the pie with a small slice.
Caller -> A small slice. And no seconds. I'll try. No promises on the stuffing.
Nurse -> Ha. Honest.
Caller -> I'm glad you asked. I have fifteen left. That's about two weeks.
Nurse -> Do you test only in the morning, or other times, too?
Caller -> Just mornings. Once in a while after dinner if I'm curious.
Nurse -> That matches your plan. Keep doing that.
Nurse -> I'll order more right now. Do you need lancets or the control solution?
Caller -> Can you hear me okay? The signal's a little weak.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine.
Caller -> No, I'm fine on lancets. I have a whole box. I just need strips.
Nurse -> Then it's strips. I'll have them sent.
Caller -> Thank you. That'll come before I run out?
Nurse -> It should. Usually three days. If it's late, call me.
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> I will. I'm good at nagging.
Nurse -> Does your sister nag you, too?
Caller -> Oh, constantly. She texts me a picture of a salad every morning.
Nurse -> Ha. Accountability.
Caller -> Accountability with lettuce.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a skill.
Caller -> I also nagged the pharmacy until they found my old prescription. Persistence, that's my superpower.
Caller -> My sister says it's my only one.
Nurse -> Ha. Now, your appointment. What did you want to ask?
Caller -> I have a visit Thursday. At ten. But my daughter has a recital that morning and I want to go. Can we move it to Friday?
Nurse -> Let me look at the schedule. Friday at ten is open. I can move you.
Caller -> Friday at ten. Perfect. Yes, please.
Nurse -> It's done. Friday instead of Thursday.
Nurse -> You'll get a reminder call Thursday afternoon.
Caller -> Thursday afternoon. I'll be at the recital, but I'll see the phone after.
Caller -> Thank you so much. You're the best.
Nurse -> Will your sister drive you Friday, or will you walk?
Caller -> She'll walk over. She lives four blocks away. We'll have tea and she'll sit in on the visit.
Nurse -> She's welcome to. Bring your glucose log and your meter.
Caller -> I always do. I keep them in a little blue bag so I don't forget.
Nurse -> Anytime. A recital, how fun. What does she play?
Caller -> I should tell you, I wore a hat to her last one and blocked the whole row. I'm leaving it at home.
Nurse -> Ha. Your row will thank you.
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> The violin. She's eleven. She's been practicing the same piece for a month. I know every note. I could play it in my sleep.
Caller -> It's a Suzuki piece. Book two. Gavotte. I'll hum it for you if you want.
Nurse -> I'll pass this time. I'll hear it in my dreams.
Caller -> Ha. You and me both.
Nurse -> Ha. A proud mom.
Nurse -> When is the recital, exactly?
Caller -> Thursday at ten, at her school. It's in the gym. Folding chairs. Everybody's grandmother is there.
Nurse -> The best audience.
Caller -> I'm so proud. She's terrible. But she's trying. Ha.
Caller -> She's got a teacher who says she has an ear. I only have ears for wrong notes.
Nurse -> Ha. We've all been there.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the best kind of music.
Caller -> It really is.
Nurse -> Josephine, a couple of reminders for you. Check your feet every day, like you're doing, with the mirror. Wear socks and shoes. And if you see any sore, blister, or a color change, call us right away.
Caller -> Sore. Blister. Color. I will. I'll call the same day.
Nurse -> Good. And keep logging your morning sugars. Call if you get a reading over three hundred, or under seventy.
Caller -> Three hundred or seventy. Okay. I have a sticky note on the meter. It says that.
Nurse -> Great. And call us any time you have questions. About the strips, the log, your toes, anything.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Percival. I really appreciate how you all treat me.
Caller -> Oh, and one more thing, does the agency do holiday hours? Just so I know who to call if something comes up.
Nurse -> The line is open every day, all hours, including holidays.
Nurse -> It's our pleasure. You're doing the work.
Caller -> I used to think nobody cared about the small stuff. Then I got you all.
Nurse -> The small stuff is the big stuff. It adds up.
Caller -> I'm trying. One day at a time.
Nurse -> Is your mood okay? Sometimes managing a condition gets heavy.
Caller -> It's good. Actually the best in years. I started painting again. Watercolors.
Nurse -> That's lovely. What do you paint?
Caller -> Birds, mostly. Cardinals. They come to the feeder and I can't resist.
Nurse -> I'd love to see one.
Caller -> I'll show you Friday. I'll bring the cardinal.
Nurse -> That's how it works.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Have a good day.
Nurse -> You too. Bye, Josephine.
Caller -> Bye.

turns.text: Will your sister drive you Friday, or will you walk?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She'll walk over. She lives four blocks away. We'll have tea and she'll sit in on the visit.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: She's welcome to. Bring your glucose log and your meter.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I always do. I keep them in a little blue bag so I don't forget.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Anytime. A recital, how fun. What does she play?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I should tell you, I wore a hat to her last one and blocked the whole row. I'm leaving it at home.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Your row will thank you.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: No problem, take your time.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The violin. She's eleven. She's been practicing the same piece for a month. I know every note. I could play it in my sleep.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's a Suzuki piece. Book two. Gavotte. I'll hum it for you if you want.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'll pass this time. I'll hear it in my dreams.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Ha. You and me both.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. A proud mom.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: When is the recital, exactly?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thursday at ten, at her school. It's in the gym. Folding chairs. Everybody's grandmother is there.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The best audience.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm so proud. She's terrible. But she's trying. Ha.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She's got a teacher who says she has an ear. I only have ears for wrong notes.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. We've all been there.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. That's the best kind of music.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It really is.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Josephine, a couple of reminders for you. Check your feet every day, like you're doing, with the mirror. Wear socks and shoes. And if you see any sore, blister, or a color change, call us right away.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Sore. Blister. Color. I will. I'll call the same day.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. And keep logging your morning sugars. Call if you get a reading over three hundred, or under seventy.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Three hundred or seventy. Okay. I have a sticky note on the meter. It says that.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Great. And call us any time you have questions. About the strips, the log, your toes, anything.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I will. Thank you, Percival. I really appreciate how you all treat me.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Oh, and one more thing, does the agency do holiday hours? Just so I know who to call if something comes up.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The line is open every day, all hours, including holidays.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's our pleasure. You're doing the work.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I used to think nobody cared about the small stuff. Then I got you all.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The small stuff is the big stuff. It adds up.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm trying. One day at a time.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is your mood okay? Sometimes managing a condition gets heavy.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's good. Actually the best in years. I started painting again. Watercolors.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's lovely. What do you paint?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Birds, mostly. Cardinals. They come to the feeder and I can't resist.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'd love to see one.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll show you Friday. I'll bring the cardinal.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's how it works.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I'll let you go. Have a good day.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You too. Bye, Josephine.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Bye.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Raphael.
Caller -> Hi, Raphael. It's Emmerich Kettering. I'm calling about my mother. Rosalind Kettering. She's not sleeping. I'd like to ask about getting a sleeping pill.
Nurse -> Hi, Emmerich. Tell me how long this has been going on.
Caller -> Three nights now. She's up at two, three in the morning. I hear her in the kitchen. Opening cabinets. Making tea she doesn't drink.
Nurse -> Is that normal for her?
Caller -> Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> No. She's always slept like a rock. Eight hours. She used to nap in the car.
Caller -> My father used to say she could fall asleep at a rock concert.
Nurse -> Ha. A talented sleeper.
Nurse -> Has anything changed? Medicines, a move, a loss?
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> Nothing I know of. Same pills. Same house. Well. Her sister died in October. But that was two months ago. She seemed okay.
Nurse -> Were they close?
Caller -> Very. They talked every night at nine. The phone rings at nine and she still looks at it.
Nurse -> That's a hard habit to break.
Nurse -> I'm sorry about her sister. That could be part of it.
Caller -> Maybe. She doesn't talk about it. She just says she can't sleep.
Nurse -> Have you tried anything?
Caller -> Melatonin. Three milligrams. For a week. And a warm bath. She says the bath is nice but it doesn't help.
Nurse -> Okay. Any pain? Any falls?
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> No pain. No falls. She walks around holding the counter. I'd hear if she fell. I'm in the next room.
Nurse -> Good. What sleeping pill were you thinking of?
Caller -> I looked it up. Zolpidem. Five milligrams at bedtime. The older folks get the lower dose. My neighbor takes it.
Nurse -> I understand. I can't start a new medicine myself. That has to come from her doctor. And I want to be careful with that one in older adults. It can cause confusion and falls.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't know that.
Nurse -> Many people don't. I'll send a message to her doctor about the sleep trouble and your request, and let them decide.
Caller -> I just want her to rest. I'm tired too, to be honest. I keep one ear open all night.
Nurse -> That's exhausting. We'll help find a plan for both of you.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. That makes sense.
Nurse -> Can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.

transcript:
Nurse -> Gladstone Home Health, this is Cordelia.
Caller -> Hi, Cordelia. It's Mervin Calloway. M E R V I N. I'm a patient. I had my toe taken off last week. And I think there's something going on with it.
Nurse -> Hi, Marvin. I'm sorry to hear that. Okay. Let me bring up your chart. Marvin Calloway?
Caller -> Mervin. With an E. But that's all right. Everyone gets it.
Nurse -> Okay, Marvin. Tell me what's going on with the toe.
Caller -> It's nothing, probably. I kept telling myself that. For two days.
Nurse -> You did the right thing calling.
Caller -> My neighbor made me. She said, Mervin, pick up the phone.
Caller -> Wait. Mervin. It's not a big deal. Go on. Please go on.
Nurse -> Alright. What's happening with the toe, Marvin?
Caller -> The toe is draining and it, it smells a little.
Nurse -> It's draining and it smells.
Caller -> A little. Not a lot. It started yesterday. It was dry before. Today the dressing was wet through, yellowish.
Nurse -> Did anything happen to the dressing? Did it get wet, or did you bump the foot?
Caller -> I bumped it on the coffee table on Saturday. Not hard. I yelped. Biscuit ran out of the room.
Nurse -> Okay. That could have irritated it.
Nurse -> Okay. How much drainage? Is it soaked?
Caller -> The gauze was wet. About the size of a, a half dollar. Maybe bigger. I changed it this morning and by lunch it was wet again.
Nurse -> What color was the fluid? Clear, yellow, green, brown?
Caller -> Yellow. Pale yellow. Like weak tea.
Nurse -> Any thick or pus-like material?
Caller -> No. Thin. Runny.
Nurse -> Any bleeding?
Caller -> No. No bright blood. Just that thin, yellowish stuff.
Nurse -> Okay. Any pain?
Caller -> A four. A four out of ten. It aches. It's a throbbing ache. It was a two last week. It got worse yesterday.
Nurse -> Does it keep you up at night?
Caller -> Some. I wake up around three, adjust the pillow, and go back to sleep. It's not terrible.
Caller -> It kind of pulses with my heartbeat when I'm sitting still. Like a little drum.
Nurse -> That's helpful to know. I'll pass it on.
Nurse -> Does anything make it better or worse?
Caller -> Raising the foot helps. When I put it down on the floor the throbbing starts.
Nurse -> That's useful. Elevation is good.
Nurse -> Do you have a fever?
Caller -> I took it an hour ago. Ninety nine point six. So a little warm.
Caller -> I use the digital one. It beeps. It beeped twice, so I did it again to be sure.
Nurse -> And both were the same?
Caller -> Both the same. Ninety nine point six.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chills? Shaking, sweats?
Caller -> No chills. I felt kind of warm last night. No shaking.
Nurse -> Did you take anything for it, like acetaminophen?
Caller -> Nothing. I didn't want to hide a fever. The nurse said not to cover it up.
Nurse -> That's a smart instinct.
Nurse -> Any redness going up the foot or the leg? Any red streaks?
Caller -> I looked. I used the mirror. It's red around the edge of the dressing, but no streaks. Nothing climbing up. Just the, around the wound.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you taking an antibiotic?
Caller -> Yes. The cephalexin. Five hundred milligrams. Four times a day. I'm on day five of ten. I took one at noon.
Nurse -> Good. Have you missed any doses?
Caller -> No. I have an alarm. Seven, noon, five, and ten. I haven't missed one.
Nurse -> Excellent. What's your date of birth, Mervin?
Caller -> Wait, could you say that again? The line broke.
Nurse -> What is your date of birth, Mervin?
Caller -> Got it. May fourteenth. I'll say it slow.
Caller -> May fourteenth, nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> May fourteenth, nineteen sixty four. Thank you. And a number?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one zero three.
Nurse -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one eight three. Is that right?
Caller -> No, no. Zero one zero three. The number ends in zero one zero three. Not eight. Zero.
Nurse -> Zero one zero three. Got it. Sorry about that.
Caller -> No problem. It's a bad connection. I keep dropping out. Can you hear me okay?
Nurse -> Do you want to move indoors and call back?
Caller -> No, no. It's cold but the signal's better. I'll stay put.
Nurse -> Alright. Tell me if you drop out.
Nurse -> I can. A few words are cutting out, but I'm getting most of it.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'm on the porch because it's the only place I get a signal.
Nurse -> I'll keep my questions short then.
Caller -> I appreciate it. It's windy, too. You might hear the chimes.
Caller -> Hang on. There they go.
Nurse -> Ha. I can hear them. Pretty.
Nurse -> Ha. A porch phone call. Are you warm enough?
Caller -> I used to sit out here every evening before the surgery. Watching the street. It's my spot.
Nurse -> It sounds like a nice spot.
Caller -> I'm bundled. I have a blanket and a coffee. It's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Mervin, let's talk about the dressing. How are you changing it?
Caller -> Once a day. I wash my hands. I take the old one off, I look at it, I put a new one on. I use the gauze and the paper tape. And the, the nurse said to wrap it with the rolled gauze.
Nurse -> Do you use any ointment under the gauze?
Caller -> Just what they gave me at the hospital. It's the white stuff in the tube. A thin layer.
Nurse -> That's right. Only a thin layer.
Nurse -> How many rolls of gauze do you have?
Caller -> I have three. Three rolls. I'm using one a day, so that's three days.
Caller -> I could stretch it by using the tape more. But I don't want to.
Nurse -> Don't stretch it. Use what you need.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll order more. I'll send plenty.
Caller -> Thank you. I appreciate that.
Nurse -> Mervin, I'm going to send a message to the wound clinician about the drainage and the smell, so they can decide if they want to change anything.
Caller -> Okay. That's good. I was hoping somebody would look at it.
Nurse -> And I'm scheduling a nurse visit for tomorrow, so she can look at it in person.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Great. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a window. Probably in the morning.
Caller -> I'll be around. I'm not going anywhere. I can't, with the foot.
Nurse -> Ha. That's true. In the meantime, change the dressing once a day or any time it gets soaked. Wash your hands first. Keep your foot raised on a pillow when you're sitting. And keep the dressing dry.
Caller -> Once a day, or when it's soaked. Wash hands. Foot up. Keep it dry. Okay. I'll cover it when I shower.
Nurse -> And after the shower, change the dressing right away, even if it stayed dry.
Caller -> Right after. Okay. I'll have the clean one ready on the towel.
Nurse -> Do you shower?
Caller -> I sit on a stool and I put a plastic bag over the foot. With tape.
Nurse -> That's good. Make sure the bag is sealed all the way around.
Caller -> It is. I've done it a few times.
Nurse -> Great. Also, finish every dose of the antibiotic. Even if the toe looks better. Take it evenly spaced and with food.
Caller -> Every dose. Spaced out. With food. I take it with crackers or toast.
Nurse -> Perfect. Mervin, there are a few things to watch for. If your temperature goes to one hundred one or higher, if you get chills, if you see red streaks going up the foot, if the drainage gets heavy, or the pain gets worse, call us right away.
Nurse -> Does that make sense so far?
Caller -> It does. You're easy to follow, Cordelia. The last nurse talked so fast I wrote nothing down.
Caller -> A hundred one. Chills. Red streaks. Heavy drainage. More pain. Okay. I wrote it on a sticky note. It's on the coffee table.
Nurse -> Good. If you can't reach us, go to the emergency room.
Caller -> I will. My neighbor said she'd drive me if I need it.
Nurse -> What's her name, in case we need to reach her?
Caller -> Loretta. Across the street. She has a green door.
Nurse -> We'll make a note of it.
Nurse -> That's great. It helps to have a ride.
Caller -> She's a good neighbor. She brought me soup.
Caller -> She also brought a casserole, but I haven't touched it. It has olives. I hate olives.
Nurse -> Ha. A hazard of casseroles.
Caller -> I'm politely hiding it in the freezer.
Nurse -> Ha. What kind?
Caller -> Chicken and rice. With too much pepper. But I ate it.
Caller -> I love pepper, though. I just can't taste much since the cold.
Nurse -> Ha. Then Loretta did the right thing.
Nurse -> Ha. That's what neighbors are for.
Caller -> Yes. And she's checking on my cat when I'm in bed. His name is Biscuit.
Nurse -> Is it hard being home alone?
Caller -> A little. I'm not used to sitting. I used to drive a delivery truck. Now I'm watching the same four shows.
Nurse -> That's a big change.
Caller -> It's driving me nuts. But I'll get through it. I just want to walk again.
Nurse -> Biscuit. I like that.
Caller -> He's got a bad attitude. But he's a good boy.
Nurse -> Ha. Cats and attitudes.
Caller -> He's an orange tabby. He sits on my foot. The good foot.
Nurse -> Ha. Keep it that way.
Caller -> I do. I don't want him near the bad one.
Caller -> He tried to sniff the dressing once and I about jumped through the roof.
Nurse -> Good reflexes. Keep the cat away from the wound for now, and wash your hands if he's been on the foot.
Nurse -> Good plan. Is there anything else I can help with?
Caller -> No, that's it. Oh, wait. Can I drive?
Nurse -> Not yet. Not until the surgeon says. Which foot?
Caller -> When do you think I could? Roughly.
Nurse -> That's for the surgeon to say. They'll know when the wound has healed.
Caller -> Okay. I'll ask at the follow up. It's the twentieth.
Caller -> The right. The driving foot. Ha.
Nurse -> Does your insurance cover a ride service to appointments?
Caller -> I think so. I'll ask. Loretta says she'll drive me but I hate to impose.
Nurse -> The scheduler can help check that. Ask at the visit tomorrow.
Nurse -> Then definitely not. Let the neighbor drive.
Caller -> Okay. I figured. I'll behave.
Caller -> Can I ask one more silly thing? Is it okay to elevate the foot above my heart?
Nurse -> Slightly above is fine while you're lying down. Not hanging it down is the main thing.
Caller -> Okay. Pillows then.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself, Mervin. We'll see you tomorrow.
Caller -> I will. And thank you for not rushing me. I know you've got other calls.
Nurse -> You're not rushing me. You're one of my calls today.
Caller -> Thank you, Cordelia. Bye.
Caller -> Oh, one more thing, sorry. Is it normal for it to itch around the edges?
Nurse -> Mild itching can be part of healing, but tell the nurse tomorrow. Don't scratch it.
Caller -> I'll keep my hands off.
Nurse -> Bye, Mervin.

turns.text: What is your date of birth, Mervin?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Got it. May fourteenth. I'll say it slow.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: May fourteenth, nineteen sixty four.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: May fourteenth, nineteen sixty four. Thank you. And a number?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Seven one three, five five five, zero one zero three.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Seven one three, five five five, zero one eight three. Is that right?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No, no. Zero one zero three. The number ends in zero one zero three. Not eight. Zero.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Zero one zero three. Got it. Sorry about that.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No problem. It's a bad connection. I keep dropping out. Can you hear me okay?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Do you want to move indoors and call back?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No, no. It's cold but the signal's better. I'll stay put.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Alright. Tell me if you drop out.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I can. A few words are cutting out, but I'm getting most of it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Good. I'm on the porch because it's the only place I get a signal.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'll keep my questions short then.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I appreciate it. It's windy, too. You might hear the chimes.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Hang on. There they go.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. I can hear them. Pretty.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. A porch phone call. Are you warm enough?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I used to sit out here every evening before the surgery. Watching the street. It's my spot.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It sounds like a nice spot.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm bundled. I have a blanket and a coffee. It's fine.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. Mervin, let's talk about the dressing. How are you changing it?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Once a day. I wash my hands. I take the old one off, I look at it, I put a new one on. I use the gauze and the paper tape. And the, the nurse said to wrap it with the rolled gauze.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Do you use any ointment under the gauze?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Just what they gave me at the hospital. It's the white stuff in the tube. A thin layer.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's right. Only a thin layer.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: How many rolls of gauze do you have?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I have three. Three rolls. I'm using one a day, so that's three days.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I could stretch it by using the tape more. But I don't want to.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Don't stretch it. Use what you need.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. I'll order more. I'll send plenty.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Mervin, I'm going to send a message to the wound clinician about the drainage and the smell, so they can decide if they want to change anything.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. That's good. I was hoping somebody would look at it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: And I'm scheduling a nurse visit for tomorrow, so she can look at it in person.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Tomorrow. Great. What time?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The scheduler will call you with a window. Probably in the morning.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll be around. I'm not going anywhere. I can't, with the foot.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. That's true. In the meantime, change the dressing once a day or any time it gets soaked. Wash your hands first. Keep your foot raised on a pillow when you're sitting. And keep the dressing dry.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Once a day, or when it's soaked. Wash hands. Foot up. Keep it dry. Okay. I'll cover it when I shower.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: And after the shower, change the dressing right away, even if it stayed dry.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Right after. Okay. I'll have the clean one ready on the towel.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Do you shower?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I sit on a stool and I put a plastic bag over the foot. With tape.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's good. Make sure the bag is sealed all the way around.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It is. I've done it a few times.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Great. Also, finish every dose of the antibiotic. Even if the toe looks better. Take it evenly spaced and with food.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Every dose. Spaced out. With food. I take it with crackers or toast.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. Mervin, there are a few things to watch for. If your temperature goes to one hundred one or higher, if you get chills, if you see red streaks going up the foot, if the drainage gets heavy, or the pain gets worse, call us right away.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does that make sense so far?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It does. You're easy to follow, Cordelia. The last nurse talked so fast I wrote nothing down.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A hundred one. Chills. Red streaks. Heavy drainage. More pain. Okay. I wrote it on a sticky note. It's on the coffee table.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. If you can't reach us, go to the emergency room.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I will. My neighbor said she'd drive me if I need it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: What's her name, in case we need to reach her?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Loretta. Across the street. She has a green door.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: We'll make a note of it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's great. It helps to have a ride.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She's a good neighbor. She brought me soup.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She also brought a casserole, but I haven't touched it. It has olives. I hate olives.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. A hazard of casseroles.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm politely hiding it in the freezer.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. What kind?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Chicken and rice. With too much pepper. But I ate it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I love pepper, though. I just can't taste much since the cold.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Then Loretta did the right thing.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. That's what neighbors are for.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yes. And she's checking on my cat when I'm in bed. His name is Biscuit.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is it hard being home alone?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A little. I'm not used to sitting. I used to drive a delivery truck. Now I'm watching the same four shows.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's a big change.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's driving me nuts. But I'll get through it. I just want to walk again.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Biscuit. I like that.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's got a bad attitude. But he's a good boy.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Cats and attitudes.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's an orange tabby. He sits on my foot. The good foot.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Keep it that way.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I do. I don't want him near the bad one.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He tried to sniff the dressing once and I about jumped through the roof.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good reflexes. Keep the cat away from the wound for now, and wash your hands if he's been on the foot.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good plan. Is there anything else I can help with?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No, that's it. Oh, wait. Can I drive?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Not yet. Not until the surgeon says. Which foot?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: When do you think I could? Roughly.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's for the surgeon to say. They'll know when the wound has healed.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I'll ask at the follow up. It's the twentieth.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The right. The driving foot. Ha.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does your insurance cover a ride service to appointments?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I think so. I'll ask. Loretta says she'll drive me but I hate to impose.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The scheduler can help check that. Ask at the visit tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Then definitely not. Let the neighbor drive.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I figured. I'll behave.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Can I ask one more silly thing? Is it okay to elevate the foot above my heart?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Slightly above is fine while you're lying down. Not hanging it down is the main thing.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Pillows then.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Take care of yourself, Mervin. We'll see you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I will. And thank you for not rushing me. I know you've got other calls.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You're not rushing me. You're one of my calls today.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thank you, Cordelia. Bye.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Oh, one more thing, sorry. Is it normal for it to itch around the edges?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Mild itching can be part of healing, but tell the nurse tomorrow. Don't scratch it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll keep my hands off.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Bye, Mervin.
