turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Aurora Home Health, this is Benedikt.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Hi, Benedikt. This is Corbin Brennerman. I'm calling about my father, Alistair Brennerman. He came home from the hospital Thursday. I need to go over his medicines because I think I made a mistake.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Hi, Corbin. Okay. Let's slow down and go through it. Do you have the discharge list in front of you?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I do. Seven pages. They stapled the pharmacy printout to the back. And a sheet about blood thinners. I tried to read it all in the first night.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's a lot for anyone. Don't worry about the pile. We'll go step by step.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I do. And all the bottles. I've lined them up on the kitchen table. Eleven bottles. It's like a pharmacy.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Some of those may be old bottles from before the hospital.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Most of them. I didn't want to throw anything out until someone told me.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Smart. We'll sort them tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. Start with the new ones. What changed in the hospital?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Before I start, they kept him four days. They said his heart rate was racing, up near a hundred and forty at one point. They shocked it back, I think. Cardioversion.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's a big stay. You've been through a lot.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: They started a new blood thinner. Apixaban. Five milligrams. Twice a day. The paper says it replaces the warfarin.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Right. That's a big change. So the warfarin stopped.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's supposed to. The paper says discontinue warfarin. In a box, in bold. But here's the thing. I didn't read the paper carefully on Thursday. Friday I gave him the warfarin in the evening, because that's what he always took. I thought, well, he's on a new one too, but maybe both. And then Saturday evening I gave him both again. The warfarin and the apixaban.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. Thank you for telling me. That's very important. When exactly did you give both?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Saturday evening. Around seven. The warfarin three milligrams. The one pill. And the apixaban at the same time. It was his evening dose of the new one.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: And he got warfarin on Friday evening too?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Friday, yes. Just the warfarin on Friday. The apixaban was only supposed to start Saturday morning. Because the hospital said, wait for the INR to come down. I don't know. It's confusing. I read it again last night and I saw the box. And I stopped. I haven't given the warfarin since.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. So Friday evening warfarin, then Saturday evening warfarin and apixaban together. And none since.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Right. Sunday and today, just the apixaban. And the other pills.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. Is there any bleeding? Bruising? Anything unusual?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I checked him from head to toe last night. No bleeding. His gums are fine. No nosebleeds. A bruise on his arm from the IV, but that was there when he came home. Nothing new. He says he feels fine.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Any black stools? Blood in the urine?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He says the stools are normal. Brown. And the urine is yellow. He's careful about that. I asked.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Any headaches? Dizziness? Falls?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No falls. He's steady with the walker. No headaches. A tiny bit of tiredness. He's seventy eight, he's tired.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Is he sleeping more than before the hospital, or the same?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A bit more. He naps after lunch for an hour. He didn't do that before.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's common after a hospital stay.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. Corbin, can I have his date of birth?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: April second, nineteen forty four.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: And a number for you?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Six one zero, five five five, zero one zero nine.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Thank you. Now let's go through the rest. Keep your list handy. What's the metoprolol?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Metoprolol succinate. The extended release. Fifty milligrams. Once a day in the morning. It's unchanged from before. He took it this morning.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Please don't crush it. And the water pill?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Furosemide. Twenty milligrams. Once a day. The hospital lowered it. It used to be forty. But I want to make sure, because the old bottle at home says forty. It's the old bottle. And the new bottle says twenty.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Which are you using?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The new one. Twenty. I put the old one in a drawer.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Keep the old one away. And the cholesterol medicine?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Wait, one more question about the furosemide. If he gains weight, do I give more?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: No. Weigh him every morning and report a gain to us. Don't change the dose yourself.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Don't change. Report. Got it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Atorvastatin. Forty milligrams. At night. No change. He took it last night.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. So the list is apixaban five twice a day, metoprolol succinate fifty daily, furosemide twenty daily, atorvastatin forty at night. And warfarin is stopped.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yes. That's what the paper says. Warfarin stopped. I should have been careful. I feel awful.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: If anything happens to him because of me, I'll never forgive myself.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Let's take one thing at a time. We have good steps to take today.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I understand. It's an easy mistake when there's so much paper. Where's the warfarin bottle now?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: On the table with the others. I'll put it away.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Please put it in a bag, away from the other bottles. Don't throw it out yet. The nurse will help you with it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: In a bag. Away. Okay.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Corbin, here's what I'm going to do. I'm paging the on-call clinician now about the double blood thinner on Saturday. They may want a blood test to check how thin his blood is.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Please. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'm also going to call the pharmacy to confirm the discharge medicine list, so everything matches.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: That would be great. I'd feel better if somebody else looked at the list.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: And I'm sending a nurse tomorrow. She'll go through every bottle with you, fill the pill organizer from the current list, and take the old warfarin out of the house.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Tomorrow. Okay. What time?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: If I'm at the pharmacy when she comes, my dad can let her in. He's fine with the door.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'd prefer you be there for the medication review, if you can.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Then I'll stay. I'll get what I need by delivery.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The scheduler will call you. Probably the morning.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll be here.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Until then, give no more warfarin. Give the apixaban twelve hours apart, morning and evening. Same times every day.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Twelve hours apart. Morning and evening. Okay. Eight and eight.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does he drink alcohol, or take any herbal supplements?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: A glass of wine on Sundays. No supplements. He thinks vitamins are a scam.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Fine. Keep the wine to that.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Eight and eight is good. Now, call us right away if he has bleeding that won't stop, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, a bad headache, or a fall where he hits his head. For any of those, call nine one one.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Bleeding. Black stools. Vomiting blood. Bad headache. Head injury. Nine one one. I'm writing it down.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Stick the list on the fridge where everyone in the house sees it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Right next to the pizza magnet. It's the only magnet we have.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Also, a few safety things. Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor. No ibuprofen or aspirin. And fill the pill organizer only from the current list.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Soft brush. Electric razor. No Advil. Pill organizer from the new list. Okay. I don't think he has an electric razor. I'll buy one.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good idea.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's been shaving with a safety razor for fifty years. He'll complain.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Safety first.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll tell him the nurse said.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does he live with anyone else?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. He's alone since my mother passed. That's why I'm here.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's good you could take the week.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Always works.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Ha. Benedikt, can I ask you something? Am I a bad son?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Not at all. You're a son who's carrying a lot, and who caught the mistake and called. That's what a good caregiver does.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm an accountant. I'm good with numbers. But these are different numbers. Milligrams and units, twice a day, with food, without food.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. A different spreadsheet.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I made one. A spreadsheet. It has the times and the doses and a checkbox.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Perfect. Bring it tomorrow. The nurse will love it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm just so tired. I took a week off work. I'm sleeping on his couch. I'm cooking. I'm doing the pills. I haven't been this stressed in my life.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's a lot. Is there anyone who can help?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: My sister's coming Wednesday. She can take over the evenings.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Share the medicine list with her. One person fills the organizer, and the other checks it. Two sets of eyes.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Two sets of eyes. That's smart. I'll set it up that way.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She's a pharmacist's assistant, my sister. She's going to enjoy catching my mistakes.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. Siblings.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does your father know what happened?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I told him. He laughed. He said, Corbin, I've been on warfarin for ten years, I could have told you. I said, Dad, why didn't you? He said he thought the hospital knew best.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. That's the kind of thing patients assume.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's a retired engineer. He thinks everything is a system. If the system says take it, he takes it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does he want to be involved in the medicine plan?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He does, actually. He asked for a chart. He wants to tick them off himself. He says it's his heart, he'll count the pills.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's great. Both of you checking is ideal.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The system needs a human check sometimes.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Exactly. I'll be the human check.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's already making jokes about me being the pharmacist now.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Ha. You're the family pharmacist and the family chef.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The chef is a stretch. Soup from a can.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The clinician will call you within the hour.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I'll stay right by the phone.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Thank you for calling, Corbin. You did the right thing.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thank you for not making me feel stupid.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll tell you, the hardest part was admitting it to my dad. He didn't judge me. He just said, thanks for catching it.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: He sounds like a good man.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He is. He built bridges for thirty five years. He knows all about redundancy.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Never. Take care.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Should I tell the hospital about this? The cardiologist?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The clinician will handle that, and the nurse can bring it up tomorrow. You don't need to chase anyone down.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. That's a relief. One less thing.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: You too. Bye.

Nurse -> Magnolia Home Health, this is Teodora.
Caller -> Hi. I'm sorry it's so late. This is Delphine Aldridge. I'm a patient. I think the pharmacy gave me the wrong strength of my thyroid pill. I've been feeling awful.
Nurse -> Hi, Delphine. It's fine. Tell me what you've found.
Caller -> I couldn't sleep, again. So I got up and started going through my papers. I'm that kind of person at one in the morning.
Nurse -> Ha. Sometimes insomnia helps. Go ahead.
Caller -> I got a new bottle last week. Levothyroxine. And tonight I was reading the doctor's note, the one that came with my discharge from the clinic, and it says fifty micrograms. But the bottle says one hundred. One hundred micrograms.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me make sure I understand. The doctor ordered fifty, and the bottle you've been using says one hundred.
Caller -> Yes. Exactly. And I've been taking one every morning. For six days. A hundred.
Nurse -> Do you remember the pharmacist saying anything about the change?
Caller -> No. They handed me a bag and said have a nice day. I never looked.
Nurse -> That's most of us.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you start the new bottle?
Caller -> Last Friday. I had a little left from the old one, and then I switched. The old bottle was fifty. I didn't look at the strength on the new one. They look similar. They're both white.
Nurse -> How many tablets are in the new bottle?
Caller -> It's a ninety day supply. I'd taken six, so there are still eighty four. Oh no, I counted wrong, eighty something.
Nurse -> It doesn't matter. Keep the bottle as it is.
Nurse -> And when did you start feeling off?
Caller -> About a week ago. I thought it was stress. I've been jittery. My heart's been racing. I can't sleep. I lie in bed and my heart is pounding. I've been so wired.
Nurse -> Any weight loss, sweating, shakiness in your hands?
Caller -> My hands shake a little. I've been sweating at night. I assumed it was menopause.
Nurse -> Those can overlap. We'll tell the clinician all of it.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a way to check your pulse?
Caller -> I have a blood pressure cuff. It gives the pulse. Hold on. It says one oh eight. One hundred eight. That's high for me. I'm usually in the sixties.
Nurse -> Take it again in a minute, after sitting still.
Caller -> Sitting still. Okay. Hold on. It says one oh six this time. A little better.
Nurse -> Thank you. That's useful.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chest pain? Shortness of breath? Fainting?
Caller -> No chest pain. No fainting. I'm a little short of breath when I climb the stairs. But not now.
Nurse -> Okay. Delphine, what's your date of birth?
Caller -> October fifth, nineteen seventy five.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one five two.
Nurse -> Is that your cell?
Caller -> Yes. It's by the bed, on loud.
Nurse -> Got it. First, don't take tomorrow's dose from that bottle. Hold it until the clinician calls you. Keep the bottle and the doctor's note together so we can show the pharmacy.
Caller -> Don't take it. Keep them together. Okay. I won't. I'll put them in a bag.
Caller -> I should tell you, the new bottle has a different name on it. The old one said Synthroid. The new one says the generic.
Nurse -> That's normal. The strength is what matters.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now about your racing heart and the strength mix up.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I was so worried it was something worse.
Nurse -> And I'll call the pharmacy first thing to find out what happened.
Caller -> Please. They open at eight. It's the one on Calvin Street.
Caller -> I'm so embarrassed. A grown woman who can't read a label.
Nurse -> It's not a reading problem. It's an easy mistake, and the pharmacy shares responsibility.
Nurse -> I'll take care of it. I'm also sending a nurse to see you tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Good.
Caller -> Is there anything I should bring to the pharmacy? Like my insurance card?
Nurse -> I'll handle the call. Just keep the bottle and the doctor's note ready for the nurse.
Nurse -> Will someone be home with you?
Caller -> My husband's asleep upstairs. I'll wake him after we hang up. He'll want to help.
Nurse -> If you get chest pain, if you faint, if you get very short of breath, or your heart keeps racing and won't settle, call nine one one.
Caller -> Chest pain. Faint. Short of breath. Racing that won't stop. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Try to rest, sit quietly, and drink water. Avoid coffee.
Caller -> I had coffee all week. I thought it was making me tired. I've been having three cups.
Nurse -> Skip it tomorrow. Let your heart rest.
Caller -> No coffee. Okay. That's going to be hard.
Nurse -> Herbal tea is fine. Chamomile, peppermint.
Caller -> I have chamomile somewhere. In the back of the cupboard.
Nurse -> Ha. I know. The clinician will call within about fifteen minutes.
Caller -> I'll keep the phone next to me. Thank you, Teodora.
Caller -> Should I wake him now? So he's there when they call?
Nurse -> It's up to you. It might be a comfort to have him beside you.
Caller -> I'll wake him. He'll insist on making tea.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Driftwood Home Care, this is Annemarie.
Caller -> Annemarie, it's Winona Castellani. I'm one of the aides. I'm at the house of Estelle Prudhomme. I'm calling from the bathroom. I need to whisper. I'm worried about her. I think someone is hurting her.
Nurse -> Okay, Winona. Thank you for calling. Are you safe? Is Estelle safe right now?
Caller -> I think so. Right now. She's in the recliner in the living room. Her grandson Dean is in the kitchen. He's watching TV. He doesn't know I'm calling. I told him I needed the bathroom.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Take your time. Tell me what you've seen.
Caller -> I don't want to be dramatic. I've been an aide for nine years. I've seen families fight. This is different.
Nurse -> I believe you. Tell me in your own words.
Caller -> Her arms. Both forearms. There are bruises. Fingers, I think. Like someone gripped her. Purple and yellow. Some old, some new. I saw them when I helped her take off her sweater.
Nurse -> Okay. How big are they?
Caller -> The new ones are about the size of a quarter. Four on the left arm, three on the right. In a line. Like a grip. I looked closely. They look like fingers.
Nurse -> Did she say how she got them?
Caller -> I wasn't going to ask. It felt like prying. But the bruises are so clear, and the way she held her arms close to her body, I had to.
Nurse -> Asking gently was the right call.
Caller -> At first she said she bumped the table. Then I asked her again, softly, and she looked at the door and said, Dean. She whispered Dean. She said Dean squeezed her arm because she wouldn't give him her check.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for asking gently. What else did she tell you?
Caller -> She said she's afraid to sleep. She locks her bedroom door at night. But he has a key to every room.
Nurse -> That's very important. We'll include that.
Caller -> That he took her pension check last week. The whole thing. That he throws out her pills when she argues. She said he threw her heart pills in the trash on Friday. The little bottle. And that he told her if she tells anyone, he'll put her in a home.
Nurse -> Okay. Winona, you're doing exactly the right thing. Did she seem afraid?
Caller -> Terrified. She flinches when he comes into the room. When he walked in earlier, she stopped talking mid sentence. Her hands started shaking. She looked at me and said, say it's nothing.
Caller -> Yesterday he came in to ask for the remote and she dropped her teacup. It shattered. He yelled at her about the mess.
Nurse -> Did he touch her?
Caller -> Not that I saw. But she apologized four times.
Nurse -> What did you say?
Caller -> I said, it's nothing, Estelle. I was scared too. I didn't know what else.
Nurse -> You protected her in that moment. That takes courage.
Caller -> I felt like a coward.
Nurse -> You were careful. That's different.
Nurse -> That was smart. You kept her safe in the moment. Now, her pills. Which ones were thrown out?
Caller -> The metoprolol. The heart one. Twenty five milligrams. Twice a day. She hasn't had it since Friday. Three days. I looked in her pill organizer. Empty for Saturday, Sunday, and today. She'd been taking it every day before.
Nurse -> Does she have other medicines he's thrown out?
Caller -> I think so. The water pill, maybe. The bottle by the sink is gone. I couldn't tell. She wasn't sure either.
Nurse -> We'll sort through that tomorrow.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a concern for her heart as well. Has she had any chest pain, dizziness, shortness of breath?
Nurse -> Do you have a blood pressure cuff with you?
Caller -> Not in this bag. The agency one stays at the office. I only checked her pulse with my fingers.
Nurse -> Okay. That's all right.
Caller -> She says no. She looks tired. A little pale. I took her pulse. It was a little fast. I forget the number. Not too bad.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she fall? Did she hit her head? Anything like that?
Caller -> I asked her three times. She says she hasn't fallen. She says it only happened when she wouldn't hand over the money.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll look carefully tomorrow.
Caller -> No. No fall. No head injury. She said no. I checked her head. There's nothing. No bumps.
Nurse -> Good. Winona, can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> February second, nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number to reach you? Your cell, so we don't call the house.
Caller -> Six four six, five five five, zero one nine five.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to tell you what happens next, so you know the plan. First, I'm paging our on-call clinician right now, because of her heart medicine and the injuries.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Second, I'm going to contact our social worker, and we will make a report to adult protective services. It's required, and it's the right thing.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. Will they take Dean away? Will they take her away?
Nurse -> That's not for me to say. Their job is to look at the situation and keep her safe. They'll talk with her privately. They'll decide what help she needs.
Caller -> Okay. I'm just afraid he'll know it was me.
Caller -> He's already suspicious of me. He asked last week why I stay so long after my shift ends.
Nurse -> Then keep your routine the same tonight. Don't change anything he'd notice.
Caller -> Same as always. Understood.
Nurse -> We'll be careful. The report can be made without naming you, and I won't be sharing your name with him. And Winona, tomorrow morning I'm sending a nurse to visit. She'll check Estelle's arms, her heart, and her medicine, and she'll document what she sees.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. I won't be there. My shift ends at eight. The day aide starts at nine.
Nurse -> That's fine. We'll make sure the nurse is aware. And I'm documenting everything you've told me in the chart now.
Caller -> Okay. That's good. I wrote some things down too. In my notebook. Dates and what she said. Is that okay?
Caller -> I've kept notes for a month. Dates, what I saw. I don't know why I started. I just felt something was off.
Nurse -> Those notes may be very valuable.
Nurse -> It's very helpful. Keep it private. Don't leave it where he can see it.
Caller -> It's in my purse. In my car, I mean. No, in the bathroom. I'll go to my purse. I'm sorry. I'm so nervous.
Nurse -> It's okay. Breathe. You're doing fine.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Breathing.
Caller -> I'm sitting on the edge of the tub. My legs feel like jelly.
Nurse -> Stay seated for a moment. Take three slow breaths.
Caller -> One. Two. Three. Better.
Nurse -> Now, safety for tonight. Don't confront Dean. Don't say anything about the bruises, the pills, or the check. Stay calm. Stay near Estelle if you can. Keep your phone with you. And write down exactly what you saw and what she said, with the time.
Caller -> Don't confront. Stay calm. Stay near her. Phone on me. Write it down. Okay. I'm going to pocket the phone. I'll put it on silent. Vibrate.
Nurse -> Good. If at any time you think Estelle is in immediate danger, if he hits or threatens her, or if he blocks her from leaving, call nine one one. Don't wait.
Caller -> Hit. Threaten. Block. Nine one one. Okay. I understand.
Caller -> Is it okay if I take a photo of her arms? For the record? She said it was fine.
Nurse -> If she agrees and it's done discreetly, yes. Keep the photo private and don't show it to anyone but us.
Caller -> I'll do it when he's out of the room.
Nurse -> How long is your shift?
Caller -> Until eight tonight. About forty minutes. Then Dean is alone with her until the night aide arrives at ten. Two hours. I'm worried about those two hours.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Is the night aide coming tonight?
Nurse -> Does Dean ever leave the house? Work, errands?
Caller -> He leaves for a few hours some afternoons. He doesn't say where. He's never held a job as far as I know.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Yes. Marguerite. She works Mondays and Wednesdays. She's good. She's strong.
Nurse -> I'll make sure Marguerite is told about the situation before she goes in. And we'll ask the clinician if there's a safe place Estelle could stay tonight. Would she be willing to leave?
Caller -> Thank you. She's been with Estelle two years. She loves her. She'll be furious.
Nurse -> She'll need to stay calm too.
Caller -> I don't know. She said once she'd go to her sister's. But her sister is in Ohio. She said she doesn't want to be a burden.
Nurse -> We'll talk about that. Don't push her tonight. Just stay close.
Caller -> She asked me this evening if I could sit with her a while after my shift. I said I'd try.
Nurse -> Then do try, if you can. Your presence helps.
Caller -> I will. I'll stay until Marguerite comes. I'll tell my kids I'm late.
Nurse -> You're a good person, Winona.
Caller -> I don't feel good. I feel scared and angry.
Nurse -> Both are normal. Use the anger to be careful, not reckless.
Caller -> My mother was in a situation like this once. Nobody helped her. I was a kid. I promised myself I'd never look away.
Nurse -> Then you've kept that promise tonight.
Caller -> I'm trying.
Caller -> I just keep thinking, I should have seen it earlier. The bruises have been there a month. I thought she bruised easily. I'm so ashamed.
Nurse -> Please don't be. You noticed it. You asked. You called. Many people look away.
Caller -> She has such a gentle spirit. She used to teach Sunday school. She makes me tea every day, even though it's my job to make it for her.
Nurse -> She sounds like someone worth protecting.
Caller -> She has a little garden in the back. Tomatoes and zinnias. She's been teaching me which weeds to pull.
Nurse -> It sounds like a lovely friendship.
Caller -> She is. She really is.
Nurse -> Winona, I'm going to hang up now and get things moving. The clinician will call your cell within fifteen minutes. If you can't answer, text me back.
Caller -> I'll keep it on vibrate. If I can't answer, I'll text. What's the number to text?
Nurse -> The same line you called. Just say it's Winona.
Caller -> Winona. Okay. Thank you, Annemarie. I feel a little less alone.
Caller -> One more thing. If Dean asks why I was in the bathroom so long, what do I say?
Nurse -> Say you weren't feeling well. Keep it simple and calm.
Caller -> Stomach. I'll say it was my stomach.
Nurse -> You're not alone. We're with you and with Estelle.
Caller -> Okay. I have to go. I've been in here a while. Dean might wonder.
Nurse -> Go. Be calm. Thank you.
Caller -> I hope she sleeps tonight. She hasn't slept well in weeks. She looks so tired.
Nurse -> We're going to do what we can to help her rest.
Caller -> Bye.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Terrified. She flinches when he comes into the room. When he walked in earlier, she stopped talking mid sentence. Her hands started shaking. She looked at me and said, say it's nothing.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yesterday he came in to ask for the remote and she dropped her teacup. It shattered. He yelled at her about the mess.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Did he touch her?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Not that I saw. But she apologized four times.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: What did you say?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I said, it's nothing, Estelle. I was scared too. I didn't know what else.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You protected her in that moment. That takes courage.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I felt like a coward.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You were careful. That's different.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That was smart. You kept her safe in the moment. Now, her pills. Which ones were thrown out?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: The metoprolol. The heart one. Twenty five milligrams. Twice a day. She hasn't had it since Friday. Three days. I looked in her pill organizer. Empty for Saturday, Sunday, and today. She'd been taking it every day before.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does she have other medicines he's thrown out?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I think so. The water pill, maybe. The bottle by the sink is gone. I couldn't tell. She wasn't sure either.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: We'll sort through that tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. That's a concern for her heart as well. Has she had any chest pain, dizziness, shortness of breath?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Do you have a blood pressure cuff with you?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Not in this bag. The agency one stays at the office. I only checked her pulse with my fingers.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. That's all right.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She says no. She looks tired. A little pale. I took her pulse. It was a little fast. I forget the number. Not too bad.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. Did she fall? Did she hit her head? Anything like that?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I asked her three times. She says she hasn't fallen. She says it only happened when she wouldn't hand over the money.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. We'll look carefully tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: No. No fall. No head injury. She said no. I checked her head. There's nothing. No bumps.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. Winona, can I have her date of birth?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: February second, nineteen forty two.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Thank you. And a number to reach you? Your cell, so we don't call the house.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Six four six, five five five, zero one nine five.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Got it. I'm going to tell you what happens next, so you know the plan. First, I'm paging our on-call clinician right now, because of her heart medicine and the injuries.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Second, I'm going to contact our social worker, and we will make a report to adult protective services. It's required, and it's the right thing.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Oh. Okay. Will they take Dean away? Will they take her away?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's not for me to say. Their job is to look at the situation and keep her safe. They'll talk with her privately. They'll decide what help she needs.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I'm just afraid he'll know it was me.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He's already suspicious of me. He asked last week why I stay so long after my shift ends.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Then keep your routine the same tonight. Don't change anything he'd notice.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Same as always. Understood.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: We'll be careful. The report can be made without naming you, and I won't be sharing your name with him. And Winona, tomorrow morning I'm sending a nurse to visit. She'll check Estelle's arms, her heart, and her medicine, and she'll document what she sees.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Tomorrow morning. Okay. I won't be there. My shift ends at eight. The day aide starts at nine.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: That's fine. We'll make sure the nurse is aware. And I'm documenting everything you've told me in the chart now.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. That's good. I wrote some things down too. In my notebook. Dates and what she said. Is that okay?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I've kept notes for a month. Dates, what I saw. I don't know why I started. I just felt something was off.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Those notes may be very valuable.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's very helpful. Keep it private. Don't leave it where he can see it.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: It's in my purse. In my car, I mean. No, in the bathroom. I'll go to my purse. I'm sorry. I'm so nervous.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It's okay. Breathe. You're doing fine.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. Okay. Breathing.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm sitting on the edge of the tub. My legs feel like jelly.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Stay seated for a moment. Take three slow breaths.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: One. Two. Three. Better.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Now, safety for tonight. Don't confront Dean. Don't say anything about the bruises, the pills, or the check. Stay calm. Stay near Estelle if you can. Keep your phone with you. And write down exactly what you saw and what she said, with the time.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Don't confront. Stay calm. Stay near her. Phone on me. Write it down. Okay. I'm going to pocket the phone. I'll put it on silent. Vibrate.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Good. If at any time you think Estelle is in immediate danger, if he hits or threatens her, or if he blocks her from leaving, call nine one one. Don't wait.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Hit. Threaten. Block. Nine one one. Okay. I understand.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Is it okay if I take a photo of her arms? For the record? She said it was fine.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: If she agrees and it's done discreetly, yes. Keep the photo private and don't show it to anyone but us.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll do it when he's out of the room.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: How long is your shift?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Until eight tonight. About forty minutes. Then Dean is alone with her until the night aide arrives at ten. Two hours. I'm worried about those two hours.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay. That's important. Is the night aide coming tonight?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Does Dean ever leave the house? Work, errands?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: He leaves for a few hours some afternoons. He doesn't say where. He's never held a job as far as I know.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Yes. Marguerite. She works Mondays and Wednesdays. She's good. She's strong.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I'll make sure Marguerite is told about the situation before she goes in. And we'll ask the clinician if there's a safe place Estelle could stay tonight. Would she be willing to leave?

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Thank you. She's been with Estelle two years. She loves her. She'll be furious.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: She'll need to stay calm too.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I don't know. She said once she'd go to her sister's. But her sister is in Ohio. She said she doesn't want to be a burden.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: We'll talk about that. Don't push her tonight. Just stay close.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She asked me this evening if I could sit with her a while after my shift. I said I'd try.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Then do try, if you can. Your presence helps.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I will. I'll stay until Marguerite comes. I'll tell my kids I'm late.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You're a good person, Winona.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I don't feel good. I feel scared and angry.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Both are normal. Use the anger to be careful, not reckless.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: My mother was in a situation like this once. Nobody helped her. I was a kid. I promised myself I'd never look away.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Then you've kept that promise tonight.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'm trying.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I just keep thinking, I should have seen it earlier. The bruises have been there a month. I thought she bruised easily. I'm so ashamed.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Please don't be. You noticed it. You asked. You called. Many people look away.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She has such a gentle spirit. She used to teach Sunday school. She makes me tea every day, even though it's my job to make it for her.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: She sounds like someone worth protecting.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She has a little garden in the back. Tomatoes and zinnias. She's been teaching me which weeds to pull.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: It sounds like a lovely friendship.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: She is. She really is.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Winona, I'm going to hang up now and get things moving. The clinician will call your cell within fifteen minutes. If you can't answer, text me back.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I'll keep it on vibrate. If I can't answer, I'll text. What's the number to text?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: The same line you called. Just say it's Winona.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Winona. Okay. Thank you, Annemarie. I feel a little less alone.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: One more thing. If Dean asks why I was in the bathroom so long, what do I say?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Say you weren't feeling well. Keep it simple and calm.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Stomach. I'll say it was my stomach.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: You're not alone. We're with you and with Estelle.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Okay. I have to go. I've been in here a while. Dean might wonder.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Go. Be calm. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: I hope she sleeps tonight. She hasn't slept well in weeks. She looks so tired.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: We're going to do what we can to help her rest.

turns.speaker: Caller
turns.text: Bye.
